subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT AID TO DOMTAR-QUEBEC AND EASTERN TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is dealing the economy of Quebec an unprecedented blow by refusing to grant a subsidy of $ 100 million to Domtar, which was planning to invest $1.2 billion in the Eastern Townships, and especially in Windsor, in my riding.
The purpose of this project is to build a fine paper mill in Windsor that would be the most advanced of its kind in the world, and the project is therefore in line with our goals of generating permanent jobs. As far as employment is concerned, this project will both consolidate and create several thousand jobs. Since the pulp and paper industry is vital to the economy of the Eastern Townships and to the entire province, I think it is imperative that, for the sake of the thousands of workers in the industry, the Government review its decision as soon as possible. A refusal to grant the subsidy would be intolerable, and the Government would be ignoring the interests of Quebec and of the Eastern Townships. This is a very important time in the history of the Eastern Townships, and their people cannot and will not let the Government mortgage their future for the benefit of Americans or Bay Street.
I urge the Conservative Members in this House to act by supporting these thousands of workers in Quebec.

subsubtopic: LACK OF MAIL SERVICE IN MISSISSAUGA SUBDIVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express the concern of many of my constituents concerning Canada Post Corporation. I represent the riding of Mississauga North in this House, a riding which has many new subdivisions and developments which are without mail
service. These developments are by no means miles from the closest community. Many are simply across the street from neighbourhoods which have existed for 10 or 20 years. These new subdivisions are completely equipped with paved roads, sidewalks, adequate lighting, and receive all services except mail delivery.
There is no reason why Canada Post cannot deliver to these taxpayers. The fact the Corporation has not been able to organize itself to a sufficient degree is no excuse for the failure to fulfil its mandate. While it is commendable that the Corporation has lessened its debt, the people in my riding, having experienced in the past few years dramatic increases in postal rates, wonder if any of that cost saving has been made through better management as opposed to simply jacking the price of the service through the roof. Other than Canada Post, no business, and I use the word lightly, would attempt to enhance its reputation amongst its customers by raising the price of the product while cutting back on service.
My first report from Ottawa to my constituents was rushed through printing so it could be ready for the Christmas season. In fact, copies were bundled and ready for delivery on December 18, 1984. Canada Post immediately sprang into action, and my constituents received the mailing last week, a mere 62 days later.

Mr. Speaker, there have been many advances in the criminal justice system in Canada over the decades, but the plight of one group of Canadians has been largely ignored; namely, those Canadians who are the victims of criminal offenders. In Canada the victim of a crime has no real status in the criminal prosecution of the offender. Reparation under the Criminal Code is often useless, and compensation under federal and provincial legislation is inadequate. Surely a nation that spends millions on criminals should help the victims of their criminal acts.
A Nova Scotia case deserving of national attention is that of Lucille Hollett and her family. Their husband and father died in 1980, following an incident that resulted in criminal charges against two police officers of the City of Dartmouth. One was convicted of manslaughter. Four years have elapsed, yet the City of Dartmouth claims legal complications prevent payment of compensation. Litigation is grinding through the courts, but everyone knows you cannot Fight City Hall.
Reasonable and adequate compensation for crime victims is the responsibility of all Canadians. If municipalities and the police avoid clear responsibility on legal grounds, the law should be changed. In 1982 I raised the case of Donald Marshall in Parliament. Now I ask Parliament to consider the case of Earl Hollett, another victim of our system.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Postal Museum was closed on Friday, March 1. Canada Post knew for several years that it needed to find a new location for the Museum, but it did nothing. As a result, the Canadian Postal Museum, which is not only a national treasure but also a very useful museum for Canada's estimated two million stamp collectors, was closed. Canada's philatelic community spends an estimated $50 million annually to buy
new issues from Canada Post. Those purchases produce a handsome profit for Canada Post, a corporation which needs the revenue badly. Other countries run their postal museums at a profit by issuing special stamps to collectors each year. Canada could do the same.
The 19 people who were laid off last week should be rehired immediately. We should reopen this vital museum immediately. The shabby treatment of those employees, some of whom had up to 30 years' experience and were given only a few hours notice, is unacceptable, and a step backwards in labour-management relations.
A permanent location can and will be found for the Postal Museum when the Minister responsible for the Post Office and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LaSalle) realize the need for this valued Canadian institution. I urge those Ministers to meet as soon as possible to find a permanent location. I also urge you, Mr. Speaker, to allow the Postal Museum to remain in its Wellington Building location-

Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, February 28, 1985, thanks to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Wenman) and the cordial hospitality of our hon. friend, the Member for Nipis-sing (Mr. Mantha), several members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence had the privilege of visiting the military base in North Bay, Ontario.
This one-day visit, which took place under the guidance of Major General Morton, was a most interesting experience in the light of the information we received on the NORAD system and its role within the general defence plan for North America.
Our visit to North Bay showed how important it is to be properly informed about the need for increasing our country's security.
Mr. Speaker, such visits are desirable and even indispensable to provide the Members of this House with Firsthand information so that they can then better inform their constituents and the Canadian public.

March 6, 1985

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) seriousness in suggesting that he would take steps to abolish the Senate, if he could get the agreement of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), opens up a unique opportunity in Canadian history to complete the victory of political democracy in Canadian parliamentary tradition. The Leader of the Opposition has indicated that he is open to the idea. The Prime Minister now has a responsibility to propose an appropriate resolution for the abolition of the Senate. In this he could certainly count on the support of the NDP, and hopefully, finally, the Liberals, if they can bring themselves to let go of the elitism and patronage that have been their trademark for so many years.
The Prime Minister should bring in such a proposal and seek the views of the provinces on it. When he decides to go ahead, let him not be afraid of any Senate veto. A senate that dared to stand in the way of a genuine Canadian consensus that its time had come to an end, would be a Senate whose time would soon come to an end in any event.
Failing action by the Prime Minister, Canadians can expect that the NDP will propose such a resolution and provide the House with the opportunity to act on this important issue. All Canadians are anxious to see just where the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition really stand.

Mr. Speaker, on March 2 the consultative process enveloped all of Alberta. Some 230 delegates and Members of Parliament from every constituency in the province converged on Edmonton to present their views on the financial statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The three Cabinet representatives from Alberta participated in the dialogue and provided insight into the national agenda of the federal Government.
The views expressed by the delegates were varied, stimulating, and well researched. This was the grass roots speaking. The delegates agreed that unemployment is our most pressing problem. We must eliminate trade barriers to create new employment and a stimulated economy. The Alberta MPs listened. This forum was an exercise in democracy.
The delegates urged the Government to respond to the commitments made on energy and energy development, to attack the deficit with great determination, to continue to trim government spending, and to stop the rise in interest rates for the sake of the dollar. Mr. Speaker, this conference illustrates
our continued commitment to consult Canadians in the formation of a national agenda for a better future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Members of the House of Commons and Canadians across the country can only react with dismay to the arrogant attitude of federal Cabinet Ministers who say they do not have to consult the public or the public's representatives, the MPs, on departmental policies. Statements attributed to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) in this morning's Toronto Star, and statements by the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Bissonnette) several days ago, reflect an arrogant attitude and a siege mentality on the part of an administration paranoid of opposition.
The Minister of State for Small Business told Members of Parliament on Monday that the has no intention of consulting either the House of Commons or members of standing committees on future changes to the Small Business Loans Act. These statements make a mockery of the good work being done in the House of Commons reform committee under the chairmanship of the Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). They reflect a growing disposition to rule by edict and public opinion polls. That kind of arrogance landed the Soviet Union in Afghanistan, it landed the United States in Vietnam, and it is going to land this administration in great jeopardy.

Mr. Speaker, on February 18 we celebrated Heritage Day in Canada with a national luncheon on Parliament Hill, and we launched the one hundredth anniversary of our national parks. One hundred years ago Sir John A. Macdonald and his far-sighted Government gazetted Banff National Park as our first truly national monument, by protecting a magnificent part of Alberta. Countless millions have enjoyed its splendour since, and will continue to do so for generations to come.

Canadians are rightfully proud of the way their national parks network has been operated over the past decade.
We now have 31 national parks and 75 historic sites spread over all provinces and the two Territories.

March 6, 1985
Oral Questions
I had the privilege of working in Terra Nova National Park, Newfoundland, and Banff National Park, Alberta, under the very capable direction of Mr. Jack Nichol when our National Parks system expanded considerably. Of this we can be proud. I urge the Government, however, not let up on its determination to preserve our historic sites, our canals, and our parks for posterity.
I remind the Government of the powerful expression on a poster printed by the Haida people of the Queen Charlotte Islands, in describing their Duu Guusd Tribal Park:
Duu Guusd is not just a land we inherited from our ancestors, but one which we borrow from our grandchildren.
We cannot afford to jeopardize their future.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The Canadian dollar hit another record low this morning, although it recovered slightly this afternoon. Mortgage rates were up by one half per cent yesterday, and consumer loans became more expensive yesterday as well. There are 1.5 million Canadians who are out of work. We have the largest governmental expenditures in Canadian history, and there is no clear idea of the Government's monetary policy or its fiscal policy. This is the longest period we have waited for a Budget since an election, in Canadian history.
Will the Prime Minister prevail upon his Minister of Finance to bring down a Budget earlier than he has already expressed, in order that we can have some direction in the economy of our country?

My right hon. friend is aware, and in fact has spoken with sympathy, of the kind of situations he anticipated inheriting himself as Prime Minister. I am sure that he was no more pleased than I was at the heritage that had been left by our predecessors in this office.
I picked up where my right hon. friend left off, in continuing the job with the Minister of Finance of straightening out the public Finances of Canada and bringing some degree of sanity back to the process.
The Minister of Finance laid out a very important document on November 8 which brought about the largest single group of cuts ever initiated in Canada to begin the process of reducing the deficit, which has been followed by a number of
other initiatives leading up to a Budget which, I assure my right hon. friend, will be introduced at the earliest possible moment. It will be based on the fundamental notions of re-energizing the private sector and getting Canadians back to work.

subtopic: INQUIRY ABOUT POSSIBILITY OF TABLING BUDGET IN MARCH

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY ABOUT POSSIBILITY OF TABLING BUDGET IN MARCH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has promised tens of thousands of jobs, and he has failed to deliver. He promised low interest rates. He could not deliver. Therefore, I would ask the Prime Minister if in the circumstances he could persuade the Cabinet, the biggest in our country's history, to bring down a Budget immediately, in March instead of April, May or June.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Liberal Party promised Liberal delegates at the leadership convention a great Liberal victory. He failed to deliver the goods.
We have started the slow and difficult process of cleaning up the public finances of this country. I am sure my hon. friend realizes how difficult this is, considering the twenty-year-old legacy we have to deal with. We have inherited an extremely difficult situation, I must admit. On November 8 last year, we tabled a very serious document and started the process of national reconciliation and economic renewal, and I am sure the Leader of the Opposition will be very pleased with the Budget that will be brought down shortly by the Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would remind the Prime Minister that the election is over, and I suggest that he start dealing with the serious matter of governing this country.
Right on!

He used the word "considering" ... Considering the state of the dollar, interest rates, the unemployment situation, and considering the lack of confidence in the present Government, could the Prime Minister at least clarify for the Canadian public what his Government's monetary policy is with respect to interest rates and stabilizing our Canadian dollar? Furthermore, could he clarify his fiscal policy once and for all, and if he cannot, could he, with his Minister of Finance, bring down a Budget right away?
March 6, 1985
Mr. Speaker, I would be very pleased to discuss the policies of the Government at greater length with the Leader of the Opposition, if he so wishes.
Do you want me to write your Budget?

I think it has been made quite clear what our monetary policy is. I set it out very clearly in answer to the questions last week and the week before. I set out, during the economic statement of November 8, one of the clearest definitions of economic policy on the fiscal side, removing some of the regulatory problems that this country has faced, identifying very clearly the areas of incentive to which we are going to direct any government resources, all with a view to increasing employment.
I do not believe there is any need to rush on a Budget. When we put down the Budget we are going to get it right, and we will get it right because we have had full consultation with a wide range of people across the country, including the Premiers, the people who will be represented at the national economic conference, and many others who feel they have a very important contribution to make. When that is done, and I would hope it will be done very soon, then we will have that Budget, and I am sure the Hon. Member will be very pleased with it.
Hear, hear!

Now the Government of Canada, will be doing something contrary to the wishes of the previous Parliament, and of the previous Government, that would support the star wars program. Is it true that next week the Prime Minister will sign a new agreement on the North Warning System that could change forever the balance of relations in defence between Canada and the United States?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He will recall that in 1982 some Hon. Members in the House laughed when it was pointed out that one in ten men in Canada beat their wives. Since violence continues to increase among the young and the old, as well as among battered wives, and since women need services and shelters which will provide them with advice and protection, will the Minister tell the House how many emergency shelters for battered women are operating in Canada today, and how many of these are cost-shared under the Canada Assistance Plan?

March 6, 1985
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter which the Hon. Member raises is an important one, a serious one, and one about which I think all Members of the House and society should be concerned and see if we can reverse the trend. The question which she put to me in terms of the numbers is, frankly, more easily answered through the Order Paper. However, I can tell her that there are about 190 homes, and I believe 63 of them-those are the latest figures which I have-are cost shared along the lines of the question she asked.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I don't think that number of shelters is really worthy of applause. We must do much more, and I know the Minister agrees. When a woman with children who is battered, upset, and desperate, has to go to a transition house for shelter, she is forced to fill out a complicated means test, if the shelter is funded under the Canada Assistance Plan. Will the Minister negotiate with his provincial counterparts to improve this situation so as to remove this kind of needs test mechanism, so that there will be no impediment for women who are very vulnerable and are seeking protection from violence, along with their children?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in terms of the manner in which the Hon. Member puts the question, she will recognize, as I believe she did, that any changes to Canada Assistance Plan agreements have to be negotiated with the provinces. I have mentioned to the provinces that I would like to meet with them in regard to the Canada Assistance Plan and other social issues, and that is to take place at the end of April. That will be our second meeting, the first one being a very brief one.
Additionally, we have said to the provinces that we are willing to look at the issue. It is not so much a money issue when a woman presents herself at one of these homes, no matter what her financial background might be, as it is an issue of violence and injury. It is not an immediate cost factor which she has to face as she presents herself to the home. As recently as today, four Deputy Ministers representing four provinces are discussing this issue with my officials.

Mr. Speaker, it may not be a money issue in some sense, but it certainly is for the transition houses which, as the Minister knows, are grossly underfunded. Will the Minister live up to the Conservative election promises and the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs in its report, and provide increased federal funding, funding which is very much needed for services and shelters, so that desperate families who have suffered from battering will obtain help?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member recognizes that this matter has been looked at. As I said, the trend is a worrisome one. It concerns me deeply, as I know it does her. We have had the Badgley report on that. There are some questions from some quarters as to the veracity of the figures, but apart from that it is a major issue. When she says that the Government identified this as an election issue and as an election promise, we did. I say to her it is for that very reason, and our concern, that these negotiations and discussions are taking place.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence. He will know that on February 14 the House of Commons Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence held one meeting to discuss the new Early Warning System across the northern part of Canada and down the sea coasts, which was attended by the former Acting Minister of National Defence. At that time we were treated to an overview of the system, but there are many unanswered questions and there are other issues related thereto that should be clarified before the new agreement is signed. Will the Minister respond positively to the request for additional meetings on this subject that will affect all Canadians for the next 20 years and beyond, and will he consent to attend meetings of the Standing Committee of this House before that new agreement goes into effect?

prepared to give an answer. Is he prepared to answer those questions today?

He said: Mr. Speaker, I ask the indulgence of the House to hear me out for a few minutes with respect to Bill C-32, which is designed to amend the present Fisheries Act of Canada. This piece of legislation is specific. It is not, nor does it attempt to be, a review of the entire Fisheries Act. It is designed to meet certain difficulties which now face us in the administration of fisheries in Canada as a consequence of two court cases which were heard in the Federal Court of Canada in British Columbia last summer. Unless we make amendments to the Fisheries Act, the effect of those cases will be to make it almost impossible to manage the fisheries of Canada, except on one narrow approach, and that is conservation of the stock and nothing more or less than that. The amendments set out in this Bill are needed for the day-to-day management of our fisheries on both coasts. As it happens, these amendments are particularly urgently needed now for the proper management of the Pacific roe herring fishery. I will explain later or why this is so.
Before getting into the details of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, I would like to provide Hon. Members with some back-ground which will be usefully kept in mind when I turn to the specifics of this Bill. In the Pacific fisheries we face a major challenge. Problems have developed there over a long period of time. Salmon is the backbone of the Pacific fishery, yet some salmon stocks are depleted and weakened from over-fishing and other causes. The numbers of two of the five species of Pacific salmon, the Chinook, more commonly called Spring salmon, and the Cohoe, are dangerously low. Herring stocks too are depressed in some areas. There is a serious problem of overcapacity in the Pacific fishing fleet because the fleet is too big and too powerful. It was built and equipped to catch more salmon than the coastal rivers can presently provide. Investing in this excess fishing capacity has left fishermen with a heavy burden of debt. With, as it has been put, too many fishermen
Fisheries Act
chasing too few fish, different groups of fishermen are competing for the same resource. Of necessity, government must arbitrate between these groups.
The competing claims include the demands of Indian fishermen. They must be reconciled with the larger needs of the fishery. Fishing has always been a major source of food and employment for native people and it has a special place in their culture. We must ensure that our native people will continue to enjoy their traditional access to the fishery in years to come. The competing claims include the demands of sports fishermen who are economically a very significant factor on the West Coast. Their claims must be weighed against the claims of commercial and native fishermen who depend on the fishery for their livelihood. When I refer to native fishermen, I am referring not only to our native Canadians who take salmon as food fish, but also to the very large number of our native citizens who are in the commercial fishery.
Within the commercial fishery itself there is competition for a scarce resource. We must reconcile the interests of fishermen using different types of gear. Moreover, this reconciliation of complex, competing interests must take place within the context of the crucial need to safeguard and enhance the resource itself. Mr. Speaker, as you will see, the amendments to Bill C-32 are needed to confirm and to clarify our authority under the Fisheries Act to make decisions reconciling all these competing interests.
Although I have so far spoken mainly of the Pacific fisheries, Hon. Members will find that the amendments in this Bill are no less necessary for proper management of the Atlantic fishery. The process of reconciliation of competing interests now in place to distribute the resource between inshore and offshore fishermen, and among fleet sectors operating in different areas, must be maintained. Clarification of the scope of the Act will confirm our current ability to manage fisheries, not only to protect and to conserve the resource, but also in the interest of fishermen, plant workers, and communities that rely on the resource for their livelihood. There is clear relationship, Mr. Speaker, between sound fisheries management and the social and economic health of the entire Atlantic region.
I and my Government have already taken steps to alleviate some of the problems which I have mentioned today. We have curtailed fishing of some stocks to levels that will help those stocks to rebuild. On the West Coast we have negotiated a salmon treaty with the Americans. This treaty plugs loopholes in Pacific salmon management that have cost both the United States and Canada great losses over the years. There will be a period of some difficult, short-term adjustments, but the benefits from this agreement will be truly long term. Right now we are in the process of developing options to address the other problems I have mentioned, such as the excess capacity in the Pacific fleet.
I am convinced that the resolution of such specific problems, and of the enduring problem of reconciling disparate interests, must be a co-operative enterprise. It has to be. These are not problems that can be solved by government decree. No one group can hope to realize its objectives to the exclusion of all

others or in isolation from others. The problems we have in our fisheries, and there are many, have largely arisen, I believe, through an inability to agree. I do not blame anyone in particular for that although it has been more of a problem in some places than in others. That problem is being successfully addressed by all of the participants in the fishery.
The House is being asked to consider amendments of two types. The amendments in Clauses 1 and 2 clarify and confirm the scope of the Fisheries Act within the jurisdiction of Parliament. They are made in the interest of clearer expression and adequate definition. It is fair to say that they will, by and large, ensure that the Fisheries Act says what many people thought it said until doubt was cast by two recent court decisions which I referred to a few minutes ago and which are both under appeal. Clause 3 contains the second type of amendment. It will permit departmental managers to make spot openings and closings. Although spot openings and closings are necessary for good fisheries management, under the Act as it now stands they require recourse to a cumbersome regulatory process. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, under the present regulatory process they are not convenient, almost impossible to implement quickly, and will not meet our present needs which are a consequence of the Canada-U.S. salmon treaty on the West Coast.
The Fisheries Act is a venerable document. It was passed in 1867. Amendments were made in the 1970s to permit protection and management of fish habitat. Apart from that, little changed in the Act for 117 years. Not surprisingly, as time has gone by, parts of the Act have become almost obsolete. New needs, new issues and new implications for management have arisen that could not have been foreseen in 1867, or even 1967. For instance, the establishment of the 200-mile economic zone in 1977 has given whole new dimensions to fisheries management.
One result is that definitions supplied in the Act do not always adequately reflect the realities of modern fishing management. Recently this situation has prompted two challenges in the trial division of the Federal Court of Canada. Both challenges succeeded and both are now under appeal.
The Fisheries Act itself does not clearly provide the federal Government with the powers for full fisheries management. Bill C-32 will confirm the ability of the federal Government to fulfil such a full range of modern day responsibilities.
Let us look at the specifics. Clause 1 provides new definitions for the terms "fish" and "fishery". More comprehensive definitions are required. For example, the definition of fish will be broadened to include marine plants and portions of fish. The inclusion of marine plants in the definition will allow the variance, for sound management reasons, of close times and quotas set for their harvesting during the given seasons.
The inclusion of "portions of fish" within the definition of fish is necessary, for example, to manage fish processing activities at sea.
The current definition of "fishery" includes the gear used in fishing and the area where fishing takes place. But management of a fishery or Fisheries has, in practice, long included the managing and regulating of matters other than type of gear used and the fishing areas-matters such as the inspection of fish, the activities of catching, the people who are licensed to fish as well as the places and times involved. Indeed, if we lack the ability to manage these matters, Canadian fisheries would be thrown into confusion. The amendments confirm our role in these areas.
The next amendments are in Clause 2 of the Bill. As it stands, the Act does not clearly assign to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans the power to manage the fisheries for reasons other than the conservation and protection of the resource. Fisheries management involves not just resource goals but also social and economic goals. Clause 2, which will create a new purpose section in the Act, makes clear, when read in conjunction with the revised definition of fisheries, the intent of the Act. It is to provide for management of the fishery in all its dimensions.
Let me proceed to the amendments in Clause 3 of the Bill. These are changes needed to refine and lend precision to our management measures. The essence of good fisheries management is control. If you want to avoid over-fishing you must be able to do this quickly. If you are too slow, weak stocks can be wiped out. Among the five salmon species on the West Coast, there are about 4,000 different stocks in 2,000 river systems, which is illustrative of the complexity of the question.
Under the Act as now written, our fishery managers have authority to open and close large areas-windows, so to speak-to fishing. However, to selectively open and close smaller sub-areas that might be referred to as panes in the window, they must get an order in council. This is a slow process and one that does not lend itself to the on the spot management that is necessary in our fisheries.
At the moment, a fishery officer observing over-fishing of a species in a sub-area often only has one option short of letting the fishing continue, which is to close the whole window. In other words, it would be to close the whole area. Some of the areas are vast and the result may be to prevent fishing in other parts of the area where the stocks are not in danger, thereby reducing the opportunities for economic returns to fishermen.
The changes in the Act made by Clause 3 of the Bill will give managers the authority to open or close any portion of a management area or to vary the size and weight limit of fish that can be caught.
I promised that I would explain the urgency for revising the Act by passing this legislation. It concerns the herring roe fishery and the Canada-U.S. Pacific salmon treaty. We have every reason to expect that this treaty will be ratified by the Americans and that it will come into force this year. In fact, it will have almost completed the legislative process in the United States as of today or tomorrow.
Among other things, the treaty creates a coast-wide approach for salmon management. Under its terms, Canada
March 6, 1985

and the United States have agreed to restrict catches selectively by species, by area and by gear. For Canada to honour this treaty, the management powers specified in the Bill are required.
The confirmation of management powers in the Bill will be welcomed in connection with the treaty. It will also be welcomed by fisheries managers in all the Canadian fisheries, including those managed by the provinces under delegation of Fisheries Act authority. It will be relevant to the management of the Pacific herring roe fishery. It is urgent because that valuable fishery will open within a number of days.
The herring roe fishery of British Columbia is one of the most intense and lucrative in Canada. In a matter of days-in a matter of hours in some years-tens of millions of dollars are earned. This year the fishery will take place against the backdrop of an unusual combination of circumstances.
Some of the herring stocks are depleted and as a result we have had to cancel the usual herring roe fishery off the west coast of Vancouver Island and reduce the fishery in Georgia Strait. At the same time, herring roe prices appear to be up over last year. In Japan, which is our major market, the prices are good. We expect fishermen's earnings to reach at least $30 million with the wholesale value for the product of about $60 million.
The prices are up and some of the stocks are down. This comes on the heels of several bad years for the salmon fishermen. As I have already mentioned, the salmon fishing fleet is over-capitalized, salmon prices have been low and many fishermen are in debt and some are bankrupt. Salmon fishermen who hold herring licences, which many do, will depend on the herring fishery more than ever this year.
In short, we have all the ingredients for a herring roe fishery of great intensity. Things move with breathtaking speed in this fishery. There have been years when the entire annual fishery we could allow in a given area was started and completed in a matter of 15 minutes.
Therefore, the power to decide on precise openings and to split the boats of different gear types as provided for in the fishing plan developed with user groups is absolutely crucial this year. Unless we clarify by enactment of this Bill that the Government has these powers, the whole management scheme for this year's fishery, which has been generally agreed to by the industry, might very well be disrupted by a further court challenge brought by a single dissatisfied fisherman. Should that happen, with the result that fishery managers could not divide the fleet between seiners and gillnetters, I might well be left with no option but to close the fishery, at least for periods of time. The concentration of fishing vessels in one spot could be so great that to open the fishery for even one dip of the nets would threaten to deplete the stocks. I would not like to have to take such drastic action. I urge the House to pass the Bill with due speed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am aware that the rules do not permit questioning at this stage. However, the Minister has not used up his allotted time and, with the consent of the House, could he return to his remarks in order to make some comments? I know he is a lawyer and
Fisheries Act
Queen's Counsel and perhaps he could comment with respect to the difficulties that were presented to the Department, to the legislation and to the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. If there is unanimous consent there could be questions for approximately 13 minutes. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister. I am not trying to snooker him. I have before me the decision of Mr. Justice Collier in the Gulf Trollers Association against the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is a decision from the bench dated August 2, 1984, from Vancouver, British Columbia. What is the Minister's understanding of how those decisions affect the constitutionality of his power to allocate? Would that be unconstitutional or does he expect there to be a court challenge on it? How does it fit into this particular legislation?

My hon. friend is a counsel of some ability from the bar of British Columbia. The question he raises is serious and also, from the point of view of lawyers, fascinating. May I try to relate very quickly to the House a complex situation? There were two actions in the Federal Court last summer, one by the Fishing Vessel Owners' Association of British Columbia, and one by The Gulf Trollers Association.
Let me deal first with the Vessel Owners' decision because the facts are important. I will try to do this quickly to help my hon. friend. In the Vessel Owners' case what happened was that the Department, trying to be fair, wanted to put the small gillnetters into a fishing area for a day or two before putting in the big seiners to give the small boats with the less powerful gear a chance. The Vessel Owners', representing the seiners, challenged that in court. In the other case Mr. Justice Collier said that the Department cannot manage that way unless allocation were strictly for conservation purposes. Of course, it was not. It was allocation. Mr. Justice Collier said that the power to manage is not there under the Constitution, but he also left open to suggestion in both cases that the Fisheries Act as presently enacted does not give the power to manage except for conservation purposes.
You see the problem, Mr. Speaker, of a fisheries Minister trying to be fair who has been told that you cannot do that under law, not because the judge is saying that is right or wrong, but the judge is trying to read the law as he sees it. In one case, as a consequence, an injunction was granted.
In the case of the Gulf Trollers, the Department restricted the time during the summer that the gulf trollers would fish, which seriously cut the number of Chinook salmon they could take. At the same time the Department had failed to take any steps to be sure that the Chinook the trollers did not take got through the water, up the streams and on the spawning

March 6, 1985
Fisheries Act
grounds. In fact, many of them were taken by sports fishermen.
The trollers went to court and said that this was not fair. Mr. Justice Collier agreed. Once again what the Department did was allocate, but not on the basis of conservation because if it had been just for conservation the Department would have had to restrict other users of the resource from taking the fish that the trollers did not get.
Again, what we have in the Vessel Owners' case is a situation where Mr. Justice Collier's decision was on the basis of an injunction. The decision is not as complete or as full as it would be had the case gone to trial with full discussion and full legal reasons for the decision. My hon. friend knows that because the onus is not as high in an injunction application.
There are two grounds for those decisions which give me great difficulty. One is that the present Act is not adequate, and that is what these amendments are designed to correct. There remains another area of great difficulty for me as the Fisheries Minister: even with these amendments, it does not stop somebody from challenging on the basis of the question of constitutionality that Mr. Justice Collier raised.
Those two decisions of Mr. Justice Collier are being appealed. I have to consider seriously whether I speed up that appeal process and take a reference to the Supreme Court, but I do not have to make that decision today. The effect of this legislation will at least get us partly out from under those two decisions as they currently operate. It gets us away from the possibility of citation for contempt if we try to allocate this summer, and there has been some suggestion by one judge that that threat lies over us.
I must say to my hon. friend, frankly, and he will understand the legal reasons for this, that I still have a problem on the constitutionality as long as Mr. Justice Collier's decisions hang there. For laymen and for those watching the debate the difference is this: if I do something I am not allowed to do under the Fisheries Act, it is called ultra vires, beyond the powers given to me under the Act. If I do something which I am not allowed to do constitutionally, it means it is something beyond the power of the Government under the Constitution of Canada. I have to say with the greatest respect that it is my view, with no disrespect to the court, that on appeal there will probably be a different result. Otherwise, it would mean then that we could not manage any area of activity, it seems to me, in this country, unless it was set out specifically in the Constitution.
My friend has raised a very important matter, Mr. Speaker.
I have tried to address it as succinctly as I can.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) has a short question, I believe.
Yes, Mr. Speaker. In this particular case it is not lawyer to lawyer, between distinguished lawyers from British Columbia. I am a non-lawyer. I am not a lawyer from Newfoundland.
A distinguished colleague.

Perhaps I might add that I do at times represent poor fishermen before the Federal Court of Canada. I have done it many times. I do so for fishermen who cannot afford a lawyer.
I wonder whether the Hon. Member from the NDP who asked the question was not trying to get the response from the Minister that he got. I was surprised as a non-lawyer to hear the Minister, who is a lawyer, on two occasions say that both of these cases were being appealed. The ground for the judge's decision, as the Minister stated, in this action by the federal Government was social and economic. It was not for conservation reasons. The Minister just stated a moment ago that the reasons for his action on the West Coast were not for conservation purposes. He then pointed out that the decisions were under appeal. The Minister has stated on two occasions, and I think the Minister knows what I am talking about, that the actions of the Department were not taken for conservation reasons. The justice correctly pointed that out in his judgment. He said:
I do not accept the statement nor the inference in this affidavit-
That is the affidavit from the Department, from the Minister.
-that the proposed allocation of fishing times in the areas in question was based on conservation or protection considerations.
I have a legal question for the Minister from a non-lawyer. The Minister stated twice, he admitted, that it was not for conservation reasons. He is appealing the decision made by a judge, a decision in which the judge said that because the action was not taken for conservation reasons the Minister could not do it. How could the Minister appeal the decision of the judge after admitting a moment ago that it was not for conservation reasons that these decisions were made?
It was a different Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I think it was the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who just said the reason is that it is a different Minister. I know he is being facetious. I see my two friends are fighting among themselves as to who said what to whom, which reminds me of another story which is not fit for this House.
Oh, oh!

My hon. friend for Gander-Twillingate says he is not a lawyer, not quite. He dissembles when he approaches legal matters with the innocence which he has expressed because he is a long-time colleague in this House and understands legislation and the implications of it only too well. He asked, why would I do this because I am not directing my remarks solely to conservation? The question of management of the fisheries on both coasts is not just a question of conservation, it is a question of managing the fishery in such a way that various interest groups are treated equitably in the harvest of that resource. Unless I have the power to do that, the entire fishing management plans in the different parts of
March 6, 1985

Atlantic Canada which have been in place for many years would come to a grinding stop. On the West Coast I would not be able to make any allocations which would be necessary under the Canada-United States treaty. 1 would not be able to try to treat fairly the different user groups. Consequently, the only recourse I would have would be to come back to conservation, which would mean massive closures. For instance, in salmon we would hold whole areas closed until the last minute and when we knew enough escapement had taken place, we would let people in as a mop-up fishery. In Atlantic Canada, we could not function at all. The entire plan would fall apart unless I could make these changes.

Mr. Speaker, I am always delighted to address the House on fisheries issues. I must say that the fishing industry in the country is a very exciting one. Along with that excitement there are many complications. It is an industry with a great many variations from region to region, from zone to zone, from coast to coast. I include the freshwater fishery and the northern fishery in that comment.
In speaking to the Bill before us today, I must say at the outset that I have some mixed feelings about the proposed amendments. Of course, it has been said that amendments to the Fisheries Act were made necessary, as the Minister mentioned earlier, as a result of a recent Federal Court order handed down by the Hon. Mr. Justice Collier. As has been said, the decision basically indicated that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans could not discriminate or allocate against one particular gear type or another. For instance, it could not discriminate against gillnetters in this particular dispute over seiners or possibly sports Fishermen without well-established conservation grounds.
It is on those very same grounds that I express my mixed feelings. I have been involved in the fishing industry in one way or another for the past 25 years. I have played many different roles. I was actually a fisherman for a while. I worked for the Research Branch of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans for five years. I was involved in the fishing business for another five years. Also I have been involved in fisheries as a politician from 1974 to 1979 in the provincial legislature of the Province of Prince Edward Island, as Minister of Fisheries. I served as Parliamentary Secretary, as the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) is doing now. I probably have some understanding of what the fishery is generally all about.
There is a fair amount of excitement. I understand perfectly well the situation in which the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) finds himself. I truly appreciate some of the problems which are out there. As well I appreciate the efforts of Hon. Members in the House in trying to overcome the problems for the benefit of those who are involved in the fishery-primary producers, fishermen, processors and all others in the industry.
Fisheries Act
Over the 25 years I have been involved in the industry, I have experienced some problems with Fisheries management. It has not always been carried out in the way I would have liked.
I witnessed some very strange regulations in different regions which made very little common sense. I know the Minister's past work in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and so on. He knows where I am coming from when I say that when we pass legislation in the House of Commons or in provincial legislatures we often think that our job is done. However, that is not the case, as regulations flow from legislation. Sometimes those regulations do not reflect an iota of what we in the House of Commons thought we were passing. That really concerns me.
One example which comes to mind is in my own riding. It concerns a zone known as District 8. It is on the Northumberland Strait which divides New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We have a scallop fishery there, as well as lobster, groundfish and pelagic fish. The fishermen from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island fish the same resource; they fish the same area. In fact, in many instances fishermen from New Brunswick will come into island ports and stay there.
This example concerns the transfer of licences. It is a controlled fishery. I understand the controls. If we did not have controls, we would have too many fishermen chasing too few fish. It comes down to the management aspect of it. The Bill will provide a better way to manage the fishery. A fisherman from Prince Edward Island cannot purchase the licence of a fisherman from New Brunswick, although it would not exert any extra pressure whatsoever on the resource. It is a limited fishery. A fisherman in Prince Edward Island cannot sell his licence to a fisherman in New Brunswick, but he can sell it to a fisherman within the same province. This has created many problems in the past.
Another example of what I am talking about in fishery management was outlined recently in the editorial section of the Eastern Graphic, a weekly newspaper in my province. Again it relates to licences associated with the same district but different provinces. This is a fisherman's view of it. It is headlined: "Licence policy can be annoying". A fisherman from Murray Harbour, Mr. Herring, is looking for a tuna licence but federal regulations are preventing him from purchasing any of the ones offered to him. It would not involve any expansion in the fishery. He is not looking for a brand-new licence; he is looking for a licence to purchase from another fisherman. He stresses that since tuna are a travelling species, fishermen are going back and forth between districts. He indicates that it is a ridiculous law set up by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. I cannot say that this has happened because of the Minister or any previous Minister. It flows from legislation passed in the House. Sometimes regulations flowing from legislation are implemented with very little concern about how they affect people, and we are not really accomplishing with those policies and programs the objectives we think we are when we pass legislation here.
As I mentioned, that Fisherman points out that he is not asking for a new licence. He is just asking for a transfer. He

March 6, 1985
Fisheries Act
says that fishermen are not the ones causing the flak, that it is the Government. He adds that it will soon lead to a lot of friction, as one can only take so much pressure, and that fisheries officials are doing things at the local level which should be done at the parliamentary level.
This illustrates quite accurately what I have witnessed over the last number of years. It is not only happening under this Government, it happened under previous Governments. These things creep in. Sometimes we are not achieving what we are trying to achieve. These are great inconsistencies at the management level. If every one of us was out on a special project, we may have different ways of implementing something within the regulations prescribed by Parliament. We may come up with different views as to how the regulations could be implemented.
This Bill increases the powers given to local fisheries officers. The process has been streamlined too much. It means that there are more regulations. Every time we pass legislation, there are more regulations. Management of the fisheries is totally at the discretion of the fisheries officers in some cases.
A study The Public Regulation of Commercial Fisheries in Canada shows the degree of regulation in the Canadian fishery. It is very interesting. I quote from the study:
Our study suggests that the Canadian tidal fishery is among the most closely regulated of industries in Canada and comparable industrial democracies. The federal Government exercises comprehensive control over the primary sector. The chief instrument is the Fisheries Act (with amendments and regulations stemming from it being made by Order in Council). Broad and sweeping powers are claimed by the Act, with more or less detail embodied in the Act itself.
That is one example. It is not just what I have found; others are finding the same. Bill C-32 will extend those powers. I understand the situation with the West Coast salmon fishery. It has to be managed a little differently than maybe the lobster fishery or the groundfish fishery on the East Coast. When there are salmon runs, gillnetters, trollers or any other group of fishermen can catch many fish very quickly. As the Minister stated, sometimes the season is only open for 15 minutes. You have to be reasonably spontaneous to manage that sort of fishery. The regulations to manage that sort of fishery should not be applied in a fishery that allows more time to make concrete decisions.
One problem that I and other Members from the Atlantic area have seen over the years is that fishermen are ill-advised or not advised soon enough as to when a new policy or regulation is brought into the Department. Sometimes fishermen gear up for a certain species only to find that the season is delayed or cancelled.
There is a difficulty on the West Coast that should be addressed. Since there is a rather short season in the fishery, how does one get the message out quickly enough to the fishermen? Radio could be used, but fishermen are not using their radio all the time. If they miss a broadcast, in some cases they could find themselves in contravention of the law by illegally fishing in a season which they thought was open but
in reality the fisheries had closed. That is an area that should be looked at.
The same study prepared for the Economic Council of Canada, The Public Regulation of Commercial Fisheries in Canada, on page 39 talks about simplification of the rules. I quote:
One cannot help but be impressed, indeed overwhelmed, by the weight and complexity of the rules now in place to govern the Canadian Fishery. We have described how this regulatory nightmare has come about. For now, we emphasize that in many cases the most honest Fishermen cannot bait a trap, drop a line or set a net without breaking some law. And the most assiduous and well-motivated fisheries officer cannot uniformly enforce the rules.
That is the finding in that pamphlet. It emphasizes what I am trying to caution the Department and the Minister about on this legislation and the management of the fishery in the future.
We have programs of enforcement. Sometimes the fishermen's associations, their unions or the fishermen themselves, if they had the money, would probably better enforce the laws, regulations and the intent of the Act. We have had the experience in Prince Edward Island and new Brunswick of a co-management program. It was extremely successful. It cost the federal Government roughly $150,000 a year. I know the Parliamentary Secretary commented on soundings and radio broadcasts and is in support of that program.
When the Minister was in Prince Edward Island last fall, he agreed with the program. He met with the P.E.I. Fishermen's Association. I am told that he said that the program has been very effective and that it is a fine example of co-operation between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the fishery. I certainly agree. The problem is they need some dollars. This could be policed a lot easier, more economically and better than by having more law enforcement officers within the Department, it is their resource. They understand how to police it, but they have to be identified as enforcement officers. That program has been in operation for three or four years. It has been extremely successful. The program needs dollars. When the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was in Prince Edward Island, he asked his Department to find some dollars. I hope he was serious and not only asks but tells them to find dollars within the Department to have that program implemented again for a number of years.
Another problem of regulation enforcement has to do with the lobster fishery. If you are caught illegally fishing lobster or with short lobster in your catch, you are taken up by the fishery officers, sent to court and assessed a fine. There is no question about it that no one on this side agrees with anyone taking anything illegal. However, the Minister has the power to take the licence away from that fisherman for a period of 10 days or longer.
I have seen a number of fishermen from different zones who have received a penalty. If he gets a 10-day suspension for 25 or 30 short lobsters, it is not because it is deliberate. It only happens rarely when a fisherman has a few short lobsters in his catch, if there is a bad storm or some such thing. Mostly it is proven not to have been premeditated; it is by accident.
March 6, 1985

When the officer picks up these people, he has to report. The fisherman may then be convicted. For example, if a fisherman in District 7 in Prince Edward Island loses his licence for seven days-and this happens in other areas of the country-he is not losing as much because the landings in the two-month season of May and June are rather uniform. It is probably 400 pounds a day, amounting to revenues of maybe $800 or $900 a day. However, if seven days are lost on the west side of the Island in District 8, almost the entire season is lost because catches with revenues as high as $20,000 can be lost. A bit of unfairness exists there. I do not know how we can get around that situation and manage the fishery properly.
I have a suggestion that I will put to the Minister today. If a short lobster is found under the floor-boards, the fisherman should lose his licence for the entire season. However, for every short lobster that is just one-sixteenth of an inch under the two and a half-inch carapace size, a first-time offender should be fined $100 per lobster. That fine should be imposed on the spot. That is fair to everyone. If that does not curtail illegal fishing, we should put the fine up to $200, $300 or $400; but we should at least make it uniform and fair to all.
Maybe a program could be worked out so that the Government could use some of the revenue from those fines to put toward more inspection and protection officers and to put toward the fishermen's associations themselves. There would be some logistics involved in making that proposal work, but I think that sort of thing does have some merit.
In preparing for this debate today, I picked up a copy of a Canadian Fisheries Management document entitled A Legal and Administrative Overview by David VanderZwaag, Professor of Dalhousie Ocean Studies Programme, Halifax, Nova Scotia. In this document he speaks of Canadian fisheries management. He noted:
Great administrative discretion allows federal officials to alter fishing regulations and policies almost overnight. Lack of legislatively mandated consultation process allows officials to chart fishery management policy virtually on the basis of plans of their own design, subject only to the advice of their own choosing.
He goes on to point out that two statutes bear the brunt of the management of the Canadian fisheries and that:
The Fisheries Act might be described as the hook, line, and sinker of fisheries management for it is the great source of managerial power over domestic fisheries.
Professor VanderZwaag goes on to indicate that the Act allows the Minister in his absolute discretion to issue fishing leases and licences and that the Canadian Cabinet also has wide-ranging powers.
There is no question about it. To manage a fishery and manage it properly, one must have powers but those powers that we give to the Department must be managed with a degree of fairness and common sense. That has always been of concern to me. When I see a piece of legislation that gives someone more power, I feel a little easy about the fact that the Minister in his own right has some control over the management at the lower levels.
Fisheries Act
In the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the Minister can be kept terribly busy with travelling across the country and dealing with his day-to-day office routine. He has very little time to spare and in some cases gets very little help from the middle and lower management. That is what causes a great deal of the problems in the Department of Fisheries.
As I mentioned previously, the fishery is a very diversified industry. It is a very exciting industry but one which certainly creates a great many problems. It is one which must be managed on a region-by-region basis. When I speak of regions,
I do not necessarily speak of the Pacific region versus the Atlantic region. I speak of regions within regions. The Minister mentioned the window. I am talking about the pane. If the industry is not managed properly, it is the fishermen who bear the brunt of those decisions.
Over all, the fishery industry has been managed well despite all the problems it has encountered. On the West Coast we speak of too many fishermen chasing too few fish. We had a similar situation on the Atlantic coast. It is hard to attribute that problem to any officials or even to any Ministers because we must also realize and understand that in the last 20 years the industry went through some tremendous advances in technology. When a fisherman left the harbour to go to the fishing grounds 25 or 30 years ago, he did not have a fish finder. He did not have a radar system in his small boat. He went out with a compass and nothing else.
Today, the situation is totally different. A fisherman can catch a great many more fish. The gear is more sophisticated and that has put more pressure on management. That is the problem with which this Minister and I am sure any Minister who will follow him in the next 20 years will have to deal. This Minister will be judged as other Ministers have been judged by how effectively he does deal with that. He must understand the fight between the offshore and the inshore and how he can rationalize that fight. It has to be rationalized because we have to protect the fishermen. This legislation at least will hopefully give him the power to allocate two different gear types. That will certainly be of great benefit to his ability to manage in the future.
The Minister mentioned the Charter of Rights and its effect on the fishery industry. I certainly hope that he does not run into any problems in that area. I believe the fishermen of the country are too important to be given second-hand treatment, whether it is through legislation or the Minister's budget. I am sure the Minister fought for more money but he lost some money for small craft harbours and things like that. By gosh, the Minister will have to find more money. I know that this has nothing to do with the legislation before us. I am rambling a bit. However, I caution the Minister that those are areas in which-
There's the guy.

In any event, we will certainly be watching the activities of the Minister. We wish him very well and we will be helpful. We will not be criticizing for the sake of criticizing. We want to criticize constructively and make sure that the fishermen on both coasts, those who are involved in the freshwater fishery and those fishermen in the great northern part of our country, are well served by this Parliament. I give fair warning here today that we will fight and fight hard to make sure that the proper allocation of funding is in place in order for the Minister to do the job which I believe should be done.
This is a very important industry in that it has an opportunity to grow and expand and in turn create jobs. The shellfish industry in my area with the virginica oyster, properly managed-and this can happen on the West Coast with its gigas oyster-can grow. We have good management tools now and great understanding of how to expand that industry. That creates jobs. When the Minister is trying to get dollars out of the Treasury Board and his Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), he should make sure they know that if government is serious about creating jobs, it is the Ministry of Fisheries and Oceans which can do that. The Department of Agriculture can do the same thing-I'll bootleg that in.
You are indicating I have seven minutes left, Mr. Speaker. I could go on for a half hour.
No!

speechtext: I do not want to set a precedent here. We did that for the Minister because we knew he wanted to get a few more questions posed to him. I feel we should let the Hon. Member finish his speech and just see how much time he has left.
Mr. Speaker, I have a lot more to say on this fisheries Bill yet.
We have him wound up again.

That's right. I must say that the time will come when I will be pleased to ask questions and I hope the
Minister will be pleased to take questions in another six months when he has been a Minister for almost a year. We will see how his Department has made out as far as budget cuts are concerned.
I would like to speak about the area of national regulations and how they do not necessarily fit the situation. I feel this is a very serious problem and I would hope that the Minister would address it in his future management of the Fisheries. A very important program is the vessel subsidy program. Prince Edward Island and parts of New Brunswick have shallow harbours and I do not see many dollars coming out of the Minister's Department for dredging. Those harbours need a differently constructed vessel. The basic Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick style vessel will cost around $50,000. The regulations say that up to 43.11 inches the vessel must be ten years of age. If it goes over one inch, it must be 15 years of age. That provision was not implemented during the present Minister's regime but this is an area at which a separate look should be taken from the basic policy in order to meet the needs of certain areas. It depends on how the vessel is constructed as to the length of life of the vessel. We either have to have a type of vessel which draws a lot of water, which basically cannot come into most harbours in Prince Edward Island, or we have to have a lighter boat, constructed with lighter materials, with a lower draught and shallower keel, in order to get in. With the latter, our vessel will only last us for approximately ten years if it is fished hard, that is, six months a year. I cite that as an example of another regulation which certainly is not conducive to good harmony among the fishermen. I have received many complaints about that sort of regulation.
Clause 3 under (m) refers to "portion thereof'. When we go to committee I would like some clarification as to just what exactly "portion thereof' means. I suppose if a fishery officer were to board your boat and find a lobster claw or tail, he could probably take you to court. I hope there is someone in the committee to give us a legal definition of just what that part in the Bill is designed for. During the last couple of days of the season, some fishermen cook their lobsters aboard the vessel in seawater for their own use. They are legal lobsters, 2.5-inch carcass size, but if they throw the bodies away and are caught just with the tails, they could be unjustly punished. On the other hand, it has happened over the years that some people deliberately try to poach lobsters. So there should be some clarification as to just what that part of the Bill means. Is it tight enough? Is it clear enough that you send it out to a fishery officer in the boondocks and he will be able to make a decision as to exactly what that means?
Section 2.1(a) provides for the conservation and protection of fish in waters frequented by fish. That is pretty well basically the same as the previous Act, but Clause 3 reads:
(m) authorizing a person engaged or employed in the administration or enforcement of this Act to vary, in respect of any area or portion thereof, any close time, fishing quota or limit on the size or weight of fish that has been fixed by the regulations.

In conclusion, I would like to say once again that over the next few months we will be travelling with the committee to the West Coast and we certainly will be able to discuss further with the people on the West Coast their feelings towards this legislation. It will have to be passed, I presume, probably before that but we will be meeting with fisheries groups. They certainly seem to want this legislation through before the salmon season. The Minister himself needs this legislation because of the court rulings and in order to start the new season.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to this extremely important issue. My friend from the Liberal Party who just spoke is, I know, extremely experienced and knowledgeable of the East Coast fishery and his speech covered that effectively.
I think for the time being I will deal with our concerns in the West Coast fishery. I will deal with what I see as being the background to this particular issue before the House today. I will deal with what I see as the real problem with allocation and talk for a moment about the role of the Minister. I will speak for a few moments about departmental officials and their role in the process. I would also like to remind this House, the Minister and those who are watching of the Conservative promises made in the heat of a campaign and which are now put in question by this Bill.
I want to speak about allocation in a number of critical areas as it relates to the sports and commercial fisheries, as between gear types and as between native and non-native fishermen. I would then like to talk about the west coast salmon interception treaty. I would then like to speak for a few moments about the herring fishery and perhaps wrap up with some remarks on fairness in a number of areas. I hope the Minister will take my remarks in the spirit in which they are made so that we in this House can co-operate and do a great service to the communities and people concerned.
As I see it, this legislation results from two decisions by the Federal Court of Canada involving gulf trollers and people who were involved in a chaotic fishery in Barkley Sound. From my reading of the judgments, not being a lawyer, I get two messages. The judge says that the Act does not provide the Minister the right to allocate in a beneficial way between groups. He then says that even if the Minister changes the legislation, the Constitution would strike down any attempt to allocate beneficially between groups. That to me spells complete chaos in the fisheries management regime, not just on the West Coast but on the East Coast as well.
I am certain that this House has two very serious problems before it. We must amend this legislation to provide an orderly management regime in the fishing industry. As well, we need to know whether that particular legislation, that is the amendments before us, will stand a constitutional challenge which
Fisheries Act
will most certainly occur if the opportunity presents itself. It could happen as early as May or June of this year.
So I am surprised that this Bill comes before the House at what you could call the eleventh hour or beyond. We have known about this particular dilemma since last August. This Government has been in power since September 4. The Minister has been involved with this issue for a considerable period of time. I know that myself and my colleagues have been asking for the legislation to be brought forward so we could deal with it, ask questions about it and hear witnesses. But no dice. The legislation is dropped in the minute the herring season is about to open on the West Coast.
The herring fishery is a chaotic fishery right now. It goes down in a very short period of time and it will go down even faster this time because quotas have been substantially reduced. There is a fishery out there worth $75 million, but instead of bringing this Bill before the House when it had the opportunity to deal with it. the Minister and his Government chose to do otherwise. They chose to drop it in the House and demand that we pass it in order to get it into his hands so that if the herring fishery opens tomorrow, he has the legislation. Mr. Speaker, it would be less than responsible for any legislator to deal so quickly with a Bill as important as this. This move by the Government borders on blackmail. You cannot get away from it and this style of operation must change.
This is not a simple Bill. It contains the guts of the business of fishing and allocates who gets what fish. Every sockeye salmon that swims down Johnstone Strait represents a ten dollar bill. The question is what community does that ten dollar bill wind up in? Is it Alert Bay or Vancouver or Campbell River or Prince Rupert? The Minister makes that decision during fishing season. We are talking about an awful pile of ten dollar bills, to the tune of millions of dollars. Last year in Barkley Sound the debate was between gillnetters and seiners. The previous Minister opted for one group and it was struck down in court, the judge essentially saying that if you open it for one, you open it for all. This is a vital aspect of fisheries management, a step in the process of redeveloping the fishery on the West Coast as we see it.
The important question we have to ask the Minister is not what is in this Bill, because this Bill represents the unfettered right to allocate fish. Quite honestly, I do not think it is appropriate that the Minister be given that unfettered right. But the real issue and why this Bill will not pass today or Friday, and certainly it will not pass the week after, is because the Minister has not bothered to tell us how the process of allocation will develop. That is the reason we will keep this Bill before the House until we have a reasonable explanation from the Minister.
We do of course have a new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. I personally have a great deal of respect for him. I know him to be open, honest, sincere and well thought of by the people he has served on the coast of British Columbia for many years. But I want to point to some shortcomings which should be addressed if the relationship in this House is going to develop into an effective operation. It was impossible to discuss
