Fisheries Act
this Bill in advance and who will make the decisions, what mechanisms will be put in place to provide for an effective consultative forum in which these decisions will take place. I am tired of seeing many communities in my riding shafted because they do not have input into decisons about allocation. The money goes somewhere else even though they have depended on it for ages, before history was even written. That has to stop if I am to represent the constituents in my area and if I and other Members of this House are going to do an effective job as legislators. This Minister must be prepared to discuss the issue. He cannot simply drop a Bill in this House at the eleventh hour and expect one shred of co-operation. He certainly cannot expect a legislator with integrity to yield to blackmail.
Another point I want to make concerns political staff. This Government has appointed a group of political staff who have no experience. These people anticipate with some paranoia a bogeyman under every rock. This staff has to stop throwing road-blocks in the way of Ministers. This certainly applies not only to this Department. You can no longer sit down with a departmental official without a political commissar from the Conservative Party sitting right beside you. You cannot have a decent discussion with people on a day-to-day basis and 1 think that has to change. There has to be more openness if it is an open government. The Minister must appear before the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry soon. The Annual Report and the Estimates are before that Committee. The salmon treaty has been before that Committee. The Committee will travel to the West Coast. We cannot get a briefing from the Minister on his general game plan for fisheries and we cannot get the officials before the Committee.
I would like to make one more comment on the Minister which I hope he will take in the spirit in which it is intended, which is to lead us to stronger co-operation in the House. The Canada-U.S. salmon interception treaty did not come before the House. It came up in Question Period one day when I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) what the Government's intention was and he said that they had passed it that morning. There was no documentation in the House. We had no opportunity to study this treaty or to talk to the Minister before it was a fait accompli. That is not open government, Mr. Speaker. We do not want that style of government. We lived with that for a number of years under the previous administration and I think that style of government is past; but nevertheless, we have an example of that kind of government here. The salmon treaty approach reminds me of the approach taken with this Bill. We have no chance to call witnesses or to study it. This need not have happened because the Government has known about it since last summer. The Minister must change the approach.
During the election campaign, and even before, the Conservatives wandered the country saying that they would have an open government. I believe it was a sacred trust. The Minister and candidates on the West Coast promised a cooperative management scheme in the fishery. They said that
for too long the material had come from 1090 West Pender or from Ottawa. It is time that the people who work in that industry and the communities that are dependent upon the industry have a fair and representative opportunity to give some input. We no longer want a selected committee that does not represent the group fairly and that, in the future, may include defeated candidates. We need a group that represents that sector of the industry and in which the industry has confidence to input fairly.
We have a real dilemma, Mr. Speaker. All the data about the fisheries resource, the returning stocks, and the fishery for a given year is produced by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. No one is allowed effectively to challenge the truth of that data. In certain years it has proven to be absolutely false after they have turned away fish at the spawning gates to drift down the river and rot. From that data they make the fishing plan. There is input from a number of sources, but none which anyone would consider to be fair. Of course, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans monitors the whole program. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction and distrust. It is felt that political decisions are made and that the squeakier wheels get the grease.
The solution to all the problems is a fair consultative body which represents the groups with confidence. During the election campaign candidates on the West Coast promised that would happen, with the acquiescence of the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser). I want to see that promise delivered on as does every person involved in this industry on the West Coast of British Columbia. If we had any indication from the Minister that a fair and effective consultative body was going to be put in place to determine how allocations will be made and how management will be administered, this Bill would have a very easy passage through the House. Without such an indication it is going to have a rough time.
The Conservative Party promised a $200 million salmon enhancement program on the coast of British Columbia. The resource is in desperate shape. The salmon enhancement program would create employment in many communities which are suffering tremendous economic depression in that province. That promise was made by Conservative candidates and acquiesced to by the present Minister. In the Estimates we do not find the $200 million salmon enhancement program or the $100 million buy-back program that was promised. Rather, there is about a $70 million cut in the operating budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, as well as a $200 million cut in its capital program.
We do not want that kind of commitment. I am not blaming the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans for this development. I think it has more to do with the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the fixations of the Prime Minister and his Deputy than with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Those promises were made, Mr. Speaker, and they must be kept in order to have an effective, viable Fishing industry on the West Coast.
A great deal of blame is placed on departmental officials, the people who work in the industry. I hear politicians, fisher-
March 6, 1985

men and people on the street blaming the bureaucrats. They are looking for a scapegoat. I believe there are people involved in that industry who have integrity and pride. They work against obstacles that I do not think many people would work against. The people who give policy direction to the Department do not back them up. Many times a fisheries officer in habitat protection has indicated that a vital area must be protected, only to have the ground chopped out from under him. I would not blame a fisheries officer for not sticking his neck out, knowing that it will be cut off by the Minister or one of his political commissars.
The departmental staff are loyal and take great pride in their work. They have integrity and are, by and large, a decent group of people doing an excellent job without being backed up. Time will tell how the Government will treat, encourage, and develop this group of people. They are definitely not to be scapegoats in this case. If the Government wants to cut the budget, it can live with the political results of that. If it wants to cut capital programs, it can live with the consequences of that. However, it must not scapegoat the departmental officials in that field.
A large amount of very valuable habitat is being ruined. One example of that is the CN twin-tracking project of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). The Department of Fisheries and Oceans refused to hire one additional fisheries officer to monitor this extremely important river in order that the twin-tracking project could proceed. That just does not make sense. It is not a responsible way to husband a precious resource.
In short, Mr. Speaker, there cannot be scapegoating of departmental fisheries officers. They are an excellent group of people. I believe the reason we have done as well as we have with habitat protection and environmental concerns is because of the integrity of these individuals.
This Bill gives the Minister the right to allocate. An interesting situation occurred in the Gulf of Georgia because of the salmon treaty. Last year the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans recognized that the people fishing commercially in the Gulf took 100,000 fish the year before from April 15 to September 30. He said that he was going to cut that amount by 80 per cent, allowing them to take only 20,000 Chinook from July 1 until August 30. That is only eight weeks and is not even enough time to earn unemployment insurance. The people justifiably said that that was crazy. The Minister said it was important to cut the catch to 225,000 Chinook and to get the rest to the spawning grounds in order to preserve this endangered resource.
He did not do that, Mr. Speaker. The Minister said that it was for conservation purposes, but in reality they turned the whole catch over to the sports fishery. That was the intention. What I believe happened is that last year the commercial fleet took 100,000 Chinook from the Gulf and the sports fishery took 350,000. Almost half a million Chinook were taken out of the Gulf when only 225,000 were to be taken. A court case resulted from that. Today, with the salmon treaty in place, the limit, supervised by an international body and subject to/a
Fisheries Act
treaty, is 275,000, almost half of what was taken last year. We have an enormous expectation in the recreational and tourist fishery. We expect that approximately 100,000 pieces of Chinook, or half of that catch, will go to the troll fleet. I know that the Minister has received telegrams from the Province of British Columbia saying that tourism will be harmed because of his decision to sign the treaty at that level.
There are serious concerns about the expectations of sports fishermen. The Minister should have agreements to allocate fish differently such as to permit Gulf trailers access to another fishery or to permit unsupervised taking of Chinook by the sports fishery in the Georgia Strait. Furthermore, I do not honestly believe that the Minister has enough fisheries officers to determine what will be taken.
There is a serious problem with allocation. The Minister has not given all the details of the deals which have been made. He has substantially limited the fish that are available to the recreational fishery and to the commercial fleet in that area.
The second problem concerns gear type. The three basic gear types are seine fleet, gillnet fleet and the troll fleet. They are all attempting to earn a living during difficult times on the coast of British Columbia. According to this Bill, the Minister will have the unfettered right to allocate fish, but how will this be done? Some critical questions include which advisory group will advise him and how will he and his Department be bound by the decisions that are made.
Another area of allocation involves communities. The Minister knows as well as anyone that communities like Alert Bay in British Columbia have been devastated because of a number of economic set-backs due to the recession. While the Minister must have the right to make allocations, how will he take cognizance of the needs for economic assistance that the fisheries can give to communities along the coast of British Columbia?
The legislation will give the Minister the right to decide what gear type and group of fishermen will take what species in what area. Our Party suggest that there should be a mechanism to give people on the coast of British Columbia a fair and representative input into those decisions.
Another deep concern about allocation in British Columbia is the allocation to native people. In my opinion there is a commitment by the House of Commons and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to ensure greater participation by native people in the fishery. Traditionally, native participation has been approximately 20 per cent but it has dropped to 5 per cent. There has been a commitment in the past that their participation rate would go at least to historic levels if not traditional levels.
The Minister has made no mention of native people. He certainly is aware of the problem, as evidenced by his good words recently about twin-tracking. Although he knows the people and the community, native leaders are greatly concerned that he has made no public commitment with respect to allocation. The Minister knows that native communities

Fisheries Act
depend on the fisheries as a major source of economic development.
Let us take the examples of the Nimpkish band, the band at Bella Bella, the band at Bella Coola or the Sechelt band. These communities depend on fishing as a major source of expected income. According to the allocation provision of this Bill, the Minister can make decisions that will affect those communities for years to come. The Minister has said nothing on this, yet he wonders why we are not prepared to pass this Bill immediately. We want some commitments.
Native people, in their aboriginal land claims, are developing sea claims to resources with the view that they were never surrendered and that the Government of Canada must recognize those claims and deal with them. The fisheries resource will constitute a major source of the claim. How will the Minister deal with these aboriginal sea claims within the provisions of his allocation process?
The fishery has been the traditional resource of native people of British Columbia. In many cases it is the resource opportunity from which they have been deprived for a number of generations and to which they have a legal right and wish to return. Taking fish is a traditional right of native people.
The Minister has often been made aware that one reason why reserves along the coast of British Columbia consisted of large communities with very small land bases is the assumption by the people who granted those reserves that those people lived off the sea and its resources. It was assumed they would be given access to those resources in perpetuity. In fact, they have been deprived of access to those resources and at the same time have a very small land base with no other effective resource base to develop the economy of their communities and the expectation of a decent future in the country. They say that their traditional rights must and should be respected.
This also raises an allocation problem among native communities themselves. If native people on the coast of British Columbia are given greater allocation, what will happen to the inland reserves of British Columbia where there is a very large inland fishery? There will be an expectation of allocation on the rivers, mainly for sunfish for food and sunfish for escapement. That issue will have to be addressed.
I believe the salmon treaty has created enormous problems in the House. It has compromised our sovereignty and its timing has created problems with salmon enhancement programs. I do not believe that Americans in southeast Alaska can live up to the terms of the treaty or that Canadians in the Gulf of Georgia can live up to the terms of the treaty. Gradually one will work against the other.
According to the minutes of the ministerial advisory committee in British Columbia, the Minister said before that committee that that treaty went through Cabinet in 30 minutes. He said that the Prime Minister never read that treaty. That is also recorded in the minutes of his advisory committee meeting. Furthermore, in a conversation with a journalist which was put on the air, the Minister said that he
realized that there were many serious problems in the treaty but the Prime Minister wanted it very badly.
I suggest that the Prime Minister of Canada owes the House an explanation. How can he turn Canada into a doormat for the President of the United States? How can he turn the people on the coast of British Columbia, who depend on this industry, into a doormat? This treaty went through the Cabinet in the morning and we accidentally discovered it in the afternoon. We did not receive any documentation or details about it until the next day. Such action by the Government is completely unacceptable.
When the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was subsequently questioned about this treaty, he said that it would not be changed in spite of its problems. He said that he would take full responsibility for it. I suggest that in two years, after the Minister has restructured the West Coast fisheries according to the wishes of others in the Cabinet, he will become the Minister of Supply and Services and will no longer be responsible for that Department. Someone from the East Coast of Canada will be responsible and we will be faced with the problems that result from the decisions of the Government.
Let me refer briefly to the buy-back program. Not only did the Conservatives promise a buy-back program, but in December the Assistant Deputy Minister to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans laid a proposal before the B.C. ministerial advisory committee for a $100 million buy-back program. This buy-back program included proposals to buy one-third to one-half of the boats from the fleet in order to reduce its size. It included selling $100 million worth of boats for $40 million to keep a cost of $60 million. They were going to impose a landing tax over ten years that would earn $200 million for the Government. The net cost for the buy-back would have been a $140 million profit to the Government and it would have bailed out a lot of banks.
We were seriously concerned about the wisdom of that program, and sure enough the Minister withdrew it in January. In January he laid another proposal before his ministerial advisory committee. It was at about a grade eight level, a C-minus grade paper on problems in the fishing industry that essentially asked the committee: "What do you think we should do about it?"
It strikes me that that move was made in concert with the hackers and choppers in this particular Government. The $100 million buy-back was not in the program. Let them root, hog, or die. The Government was simply here in the business to save money. "Let them root, hog, or die", meaning the fishermen on the West Coast of British Columbia." It does not matter that they are suffering. We, the Government, are here to save money and we simply are not going to get involved in the buy-back".
That is my supposition, Mr. Speaker, but when I look at the type of paper that was put before that advisory committee, what other conclusions can you come to? The Minister should be standing up in this House telling us what his intentions are
March 6, 1985

about the buy-back so people can make some decisions about their lives in an orderly manner.
I want to speak briefly about the herring industry on the coast of British Columbia. It is a $75 million industry this year. Again, the quota is reduced from something in the order of 30,000 tonnes to about 18,000 tonnes. There will be less money for people this year. It will happen faster this year. We contacted every major user group in the herring industry this year and they knew the difficulties. They said months before they had made a herring fishing plan. Every major industry group will stick to that plan. We were assured of this by every group. They said that they would not have time to interfere with it.
When the Minister said it could collapse, he was wrong. The groups in it are prepared to co-operate and get the herring fishery done. Each one of those user groups to whom we talked said not to pass that Bill, that the Bill contains the guts of a fisheries management program. They asked who will make the decision to allocate fish to them or to the other users in the herring industry, in the salmon industry with other marine plants and animals? Who will make the decision about ocean ranching, about area licensing, about license limitation? This is the whole process of allocation.
This Bill provides that unfettered right to the Minister. That is what we are about today. That is what has to be decided upon. The Minister has to stand up in this House and tell us who is he going to consult. What are the mechanisms? Will they be fair? Will they be representative? Will they consider communities and people involved in the industry? All of that is absolutely imperative.
There are a couple more areas, and I put these up as a matter of fairness in the fishing industry, things which the Minister has to talk about before this House, before the committee, or privately. We have a situation called the "no net loss of habitat". The Minister has been around touting that his policy is a net gain of habitat. He thinks by allowing industrial despoilers of the environment to wreck a piece of fish habitat that you can create an artificial piece of fish habitat that will replace what is lost.
Let us now look at the Fraser River. I was born in a city beside the Fraser River. I lived on that river as a kid, and worked on it as a young adult. I know it very well. I did not get back to it for 15 years and I could not believe what had been done to it. The trifurcation program channelized the river so one no longer has to dredge it. It speeded up the river. This has now caused a stress on returning salmon. The pollution in the river is astounding. There are poisons that run into it from sewage, industrial plants and dumps along side its banks. It is astounding, Mr. Speaker. They say each one when considered individually is a small increment of despoilage of the river. It only creates a small increment of stress. When one adds the effect of the trifurcation program and all that over-running of sewage, it is no longer a small increment of stress. We can use the example of the City of Vancouver which has been told to spend $75 million to clean up the Iona sewage plant because it is polluting the mouth of the river. But every community up
Fisheries Act
and down the river is virtually doing the same thing. So we have pollution, poisons, and trifurcation. Then along comes the filling in of marshes because the land is needed. The land is near shipping and transportation areas. It is also juvenile rearing ground. That creates an additional stress on the world's largest salmon river.
What about the double-tracking of the CN? The Department of Fisheries and Oceans comes before us and says that we have CN studies and other older studies that say this is incrementally not going to be of great impact. But the Department of Fisheries and Oceans did not look at the fact that CP will want to double-track. It did not look at the cumulative load on that whole river as more and more and more things take place.
You cannot replace that kind of loss of habitat, Mr. Speaker, because we will not know that it happened until way in the future as that stress builds and reacts on the species. They may fill in a small juvenile rearing area. That is great, but the total impact on that river is substantial and it is continuing to get worse every year.
Then there is the Quinsam coal project, a no net loss of habitat. The company intends to build an open pit coal mine at the head of a major hatchery on the Quinsam River. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans said that it did not have the staff to monitor the effects of this coal mine. The people said they did not really know what was going on because they will not be given the staff or the resources. The Department said that if the mine does not wipe out that hatchery or place an enormous stress on the river, it will certainly not be because the Department was able to detect it.
Next is the Rivers Inlet which is one of the largest Sockeye areas on the coast of British Columbia. Rivers Inlet and the Owikeno Lake area are being logged out. The rivers and streams behind in which salmon spawn and rear are affected. This Department will not become involved in integrated resource management studies because I do not think it likes to hear the results. I do not think it has the resources to enforce the requirements anyway to protect those habitats, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister has known that loss of habitat, the invention of Peter Pearce, is not applicable. It is not effective. It is a complete sell-out of the environment of British Columbia. It must stop. Even though the Department is operating on that basis, the Minister's deputy admitted that the Department has not even developed that policy.
Another point is fairness concerning small craft harbours. British Columbia out of the small craft harbours budget will get from $2 million to $3 million this year. It generally gets $6 million. Six million dollars hardly paints and maintains the wharves. We need a priorized list of the harbours that are going to receive money in the order that it becomes available. We need a decent budget.
On the West Coast of Canada fishermen pay for every foot of moorage no matter what they tie to the dock. It is grossly unfair that this Government in cost recovery wants to increase

March 6, 1985
Fisheries Act
that from 200 per cent to 500 per cent of an already expensive cost in a diminished economy. Yet their brothers and sisters on the East Coast get free moorage for quite a few categories of vessels. That is grossly unfair. I think we have to give the same consideration to our fishermen on the West Coast as that provided to our fishermen on the East Coast.
My last point concerns insurance. In this philosophical fixation which the Conservative Government has about the private sector and the sanctity of the free market, fishermen and vessel owners on both coasts have a serious problem with insurance. I think it is imperative that this Government not give up coverage of those fishing vessels. Without it there will be severe difficulty. Some people will sail without insurance. Some people will run into extreme difficulty without it. I understand this matter is before the Minister now. Those groups to whom I have spoken in the fishing industry on the coast of British Columbia are absolutely adamant that that fishing vessel insurance program stay in place and not be changed and that it is a matter of serious concern. If the Minister would like to hear that from user groups themselves, they are prepared to come to Ottawa now.
In summary, I think this Bill before us today is critical. We will over the coming days debate it. I think the style of the Minister has got to change in order to develop openness and some element of trust so we can deal expeditiously with a Bill like this, and that we also have time to study it fairly. What happened in that salmon treaty process is intolerable, but the good news is that the herring fishing will go ahead without this particular legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I should like to draw to the attention of the House that we are now entering the second phase of the debate, which means that according to Standing Order 35(2) Hon. Members will be allowed to make 20-minute speeches, followed by the 10-minute question and comment period.

Mr. Speaker, I was certainly pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) close his remarks on a positive note when he spoke about the herring fishery. Everything else he said about the remarks of the Minister was very negative.
And he was right on.

I do not believe he was in all cases. He suggested that the Minister did not speak about the native people. I happen to have a copy of the Minister's speech-and I heard him-and right on the first page he spoke about native people, Indian people. I suggest the Hon. Member should look at Hansard at the first opportunity to see what the Minister said.
I have no difficulty in expressing my support for the amendments to the Fisheries Act proposed in Bill C-32. As most Hon. Members in the House know, the fishery in my province
has been, is and always will be the main industry. In his remarks the Minister said that the passage of this Bill was a matter of particular urgency on the Pacific coast. He also said that the issues addressed by these amendments are very live issues in the Canadian fishery. I concur, and I would like to add that they are crucial in the Atlantic region.
One of the objectives of the Bill is to ensure that the objective of fisheries management does not end with the protection and conservation of the resource. We want to protect stocks, the raw material base of the fishery, but not as an end in itself. We do so in order to realize certain benefits for society. We cannot ignore social and economic situations in our management of the fishery. They are part of the reality of the fishing business. We manage the fishery for the benefit of fishermen, plant workers and fishing communities. In fact, we manage it in the interests of the country as a whole. Whether we are talking about controlling fishing effort or stipulating a certain net mesh size in a given fishery, or allocating fish between fleet sectors, the principle is the same. I suspect this was realized in 1867, and that the only reason it was not made more explicit at the time was that it seemed self-evident. I think it is safe to say that the people who drafted the original Act knew why and on whose behalf they wanted the stocks protected.
Certainly we in Atlantic Canada, the region in which the Canadian fishing industry was born, have never had any reason to be confused about the relationship of good fisheries management to the social and economic health of our region. If we were ever tempted to forget it, we received painful reminders. I am thinking, for instance, of the depletion of groundfish stock due to over-fishing in the days before the 200-mile limit was established.
Even today, with Canadian jurisdiction in place, we know that the health and productivity of the fisheries depend on our ability to exercise the comprehensive management powers which these amendments clarify. For several years now groundfish stocks have been managed by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans on the basis of a comprehensive annual plan. Under this plan, quotas are set and portions of that total are assigned to vessels of different types-so much for vessels over 100 feet, so much for vessels between 65 and 100 feet, so much for vessels using fixed and mobile gear, and so on.
That approach has been further refined. In the groundfish trawler fleet and the herring purse seiner fleet, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans now make allocations of the total quota, not just to fleets but to individuals and companies. This approach to some extent is also for smaller boats, especially in the Gulf region. These measures are basic to the management of the Atlantic fisheries. If the act as it stands does not make that authority clear, if it is likely to be challenged on the basis of inexplicit language, the sooner we remove the ambiguities the better. I urge early consideration and passage of the Bill by the House.

Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity beforehand to read the speech of the Minister. I should like to direct a question to the Hon. Member concerning the basis of the
March 6, 1985

allocation to native people. A very serious problem arose at the mouth of the Qualicum River where there is a large terminal fishery and a huge fleet. At the end of the year fishermen who want one last crack at earning an income, be they gillnetters or seiners, are at the mouth of that river trying to catch fish on their way out. It is my understanding that last year the Minister of Fisheries wanted to allocate surplus fish to an Indian band but he could not do it because the law had changed. Therefore he decided to turn the surplus fish over to Crown Assets Disposal to get rid of them and only allowed one bidder, the Indian band, and it took the fish.
That is a very unusual procedure, but nevertheless the question becomes: Should the fish have gone to the commercial fishery or to the Indian band? Without making a judgment on whom they should go to, I want to illustrate that allocation is a complex problem. The Minister never mentioned a word about the nature of allocation to native people. They have serious complaints and serious economic problems, yet he rose and made some fairly euphemistic statements. There was not a shred of content upon which they could base any serious hope. Perhaps the previous speaker might want to comment on this.

Mr. Speaker, it is very evident from the fact that the Minister introduced amendments to the Act that he is aware he did not have the power as described by the Hon. Member. This is the reason he brought in those amendments, so that he would have the power to make allocations to people from different regions. I think that is very evident. I am sure the Minister is more familiar with the incident to which the Hon. Member referred than I am, coming from the East Coast.
I want to assure him that when I am on the West Coast very shortly with the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, I will have an opportunity to learn more about that part of the country. I am sure that his colleagues from his Party will endeavour to tell me all about their province so that I will be more informed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, a very short question.
Mr. Speaker, I always notice you say to me "a very short question".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The only reason I mention that is no matter what I say, the Hon. Member seems to take three or four minutes. I would hope that he would endeavour to help because there are other people who would like to ask questions. Therefore, if I do get a short statement, question or comment, somebody else may be able to ask a question.

Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it is the quality of the question that I ask. The hon. gentleman who just spoke is very knowledgeable of the fishery. There is not a person in this Chamber who would deny that. I want to ask him a basic
Fisheries Act
question. This Bill is all about a problem that is basic between gillnetters and seiners. There is a basic question here. No matter what part of the country you go to, you find a dispute between gillnetters and seiners, gillnets with the nets down to the bottom, anchored on top of the water, and the seiners with the big net that captures the fish. Why does the Hon. Member think there is such a dispute? Does he side with the finding sometimes of the scientists which is directly contrary to the opinions of both the seiners and the gillnetters? There are really two questions. Can he just explain to the House why we have this conflict?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps some people in my riding will be offended by what I am about to say, but I think the reason there are conflicts between people fishing on a dragger and people fishing with gillnets is that humans have a tendency to be a little bit jealous, and because the regulations permitting people to set gear in certain areas conflict with the ability of other people to fish. If I were to speak about gillnetting, which I have done, people set out their gillnets, a draggerman comes along and he wants to fish because it is good fishing ground. Sometimes he might inadvertently take some of the fixed gear away, not because he wants to hurt his fellow fisherman, but because sometimes as a result of sea conditions and visibility he is not able to see the markers for the fixed gear. I am sure that those problems will always exist. It will be impossible for any Minister of Fisheries to be able to say that gear will be fixed there, that everybody has to stay so many miles away from it and people will not encroach on that fixed gear.
On the other question, it would be difficult for me to condemn scientists who sometimes may make errors in setting the amount of fish allowed to be caught, the quotas for certain species. I am sure they have made mistakes. I am sure that fishermen overestimate the stocks too. There will be friction when there are more and more people depending on the fishery for their livelihood and there is not enough of that specific type of fish to fill the needs of all the fishermen. They are going to be critical of the scientists who sometimes make recommendations to the Minister when he is setting the allocation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate on a short supplementary question.

Mr. Speaker, a very short one. In the opening of his last answer, the Hon. Member said that he was going to say something that perhaps some fishermen will not like. I am now going to ask him to say something that perhaps the Minister will not like. Did he suspect that the federal Department of Fisheries did not have the authority to do what it did under the existing Act, thereby giving rise to this legislation today? In his vast experience, did he suspect that? Did his cohorts, his fellow skippers, mention to him that perhaps the federal Department of Fisheries was acting outside of the law and that it should be tested in court?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know if I would be offending the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
March 6, 1985
Fisheries Act
Fraser) if I gave my hon. friend a truthful answer, which I am sure he wants, but I would certainly be criticizing previous Ministers of Fisheries. Yes, I did suspect that the Minister of Fisheries did not have authority. In fact, I had been asked on a number of occasions if I would be willing to be the scapegoat, to go out and catch fish against the law, because a lot of people believed it. I am glad that the Minister has brought forward this amendment.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to say that I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Concep-tion (Mr. Johnson) has participated in this debate. I do not know if we have ever had a practising fisherman from my province, but we now have one in the Chamber. I may say, I hope without offence to my colleague from Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Baker), that not only is he and was he an expert fisherman, but he is fast becoming fast on his feet in this Chamber and on his way to becoming a parliamentarian. I think my friend from Gander-Twillingate would agree.
Having said that, I have 20 minutes in which to put some things on the record that I think are very important. Basically, this amendment gives the power to the Government to do presumably what it has been doing. It reminds me of a quote from Pope, talking about beauty. He said:
True wit is Nature to advantage dress'd,
What oft was thought, but ne'er so well express'd.
I do not know how beautiful what we have from the Minister today is, but it is what was often thought "but n'er so well express'd".
What is happening here, and we must be aware of this, is that this amendment is about power. It is an allocation of power to officials. The Minister said in his remarks that previously officials would have to get order in council approval for certain closures, and that is true. That will no longer be the case. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) is already the most powerful Minister in the Government in terms of the Act which he administers and for which he is responsible. He is now enshrining in law more power. That is good if that power is used well. It is good if we have good officials and good bureaucrats, and we do.
I want to take the time to say that the officials and the people who work in the Department of Fisheries here in Ottawa and in my region have been faithful, competent and good public servants. However, that does not say that at some point there may be officials who are over-zealous and insensitive. There has to be some sort of protection against that over-zealousness and insensitivity. We in this country are not ruled by officials and bureaucrats. We are ruled by a Government which is responsible to people. As long as we have good officials, this law is good.
We are talking about power, not only over fish and fish stocks and allocations, but power over people's lives. The island of Newfoundland was settled as a result of the fish stocks around our shore. Our culture and our way of life is built on the fishery. It is of no mean importance to us. It is of fundamental importance. This House should recognize that what we are talking about here today is not simply power over fish stocks and over fish processing. It is power over people's lives and over communities. That should be clearly understood. It is how that power is shared that is important to me.
This amendment gives the Department more power. It gives it power to open and close sections and power to allocate fish stocks to provinces. It gives the Department the right in law to allocate resources from one area to people who live in another area. As I say, it is important to us how this power is used.
The Premier of Newfoundland has heretofore put in very graphic and dramatic terms the fact that the northern cod stocks of the Hamilton Banks off the coast of Labrador and the northern coast of Newfoundland are very important to Newfoundland. He has claimed it is of such fundamental importance to us that he has said from time to time that it is more important to us than the oil off our shores. If that is the case, then he wants an assurance that those northern cod stocks are to be the priority of Newfoundland and Labrador fishermen. However, other people from other provinces fish in that area as well. Newfoundland fishermen and the Premier are very concerned that their priority be adhered to.
It is true that Newfoundlanders fish off the Scotian shelf. We do not want to balkanize the fishery in Canada. I point this out because I think it is very important in this debate that we understand that the possibility for balkanization exists. I will want an assurance that this power, if it is given, will be used properly, fairly and in the best interests of the people I represent.
As well, the Department has power to restrict fisheries in certain bays and in certain sections of certain bays. That power will be enshrined in this legislation. My friend, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, alluded to the fact that certain small-boat fishermen and certain inshore fishermen have been at the mercy of larger vessels, of herring seiners and even of long liners that fish in the same grounds. A man with a 45-foot or 60-foot long liner can fish in the same area as a man with an 18 or 25-foot boat. There are inequalities.
The Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception alluded in his answer to the fact that between human beings there are jealousies and apprehensions. That is true but the Government is there to see that all people are treated fairly whether they are small-boat fishermen or large-boat fishermen. I hope that this power will be used to see that those who are disadvantaged, who do not have the larger vessels and do not have access to the deep sea fishery are protected by this law and that herring seiners and long liners are somehow restricted in their ability to fish small inshore stocks in small inshore regions.
March 6, 1985

If we are to give more power as this Bill does to the Government and the officials, I would ask how we are going to assure ourselves that the power is shared equally by the federal Government, the provincial Government and the fishermen themselves. There is only so much power to go around. If power is given to one group, it is automatically taken from another. I repeat that the Premier of Newfoundland has said that the fishery is very important to us. He has asked from time to time for more control over the Newfoundland fishery. There is no assurance here that he will get the kind of input that he requires. Moreover, there is no assurance here that the fishermen themselves who are most affected will have any more control over their own lives. I worry about the acquisition of more power by officials because I fear that it means less power to fishermen, those wose lives are most affected.
In his speech the Minister spoke about a fisheries policy and the 200-mile limit. I second his thoughts on those matters. The 200-mile limit has been a godsend to us in Newfoundland. I am proud that it was this Party that brought in the 200-mile limit. As a result of that measure, the fish stocks off Newfoundland and Labrador are now in much better shape than they were previously.
The 200-mile limit and the fisheries policy has been put in place. We will have to wait to see what the position is of the present Government on the utilization of those fish stocks and the processing of the fish that is caught. This Bill tells us nothing about what the policy of the Government or the Minister is with regard to the prosecution of the fishery.
I would like to see a management policy brought forward at an early stage. I particularly want to know what the Minister will do, when he will have the legal power to allocate stocks, about the allocation of certain stocks to what is known as resource-short plants. Following on the recommendations of the Kirby report, the Government adopted certain policies. One of those recommendations which was accepted was that an allocation of fish stocks be put aside for what is known as resource-short plants. There were plants in certain areas that had access to the deep sea fishery but there were plants in other areas, like the northeast coast of Newfoundland, that did not have access to deep sea fisheries at the time and were dependent on the inshore fishery. If the inshore fishery were to fail for any reason, those plants would be in serious economic trouble and people would be laid off. There must be allocations to those small inshore plants from the deep sea fishery. I would like to know what the Government and the Ministry will do about that.
I would like a fisheries policy brought forward at the earliest possible opportunity. I believe the Minister is a well-meaning and sincere Minister. I hope that we will be able to have a full discussion with him as to the nature of his policy. So far, if we are to judge by the Government's record, the policies have not been all that great. What we in my province have seen in the fisheries so far is cut-backs which have inhibited the ability of fishermen to carry on their livelihood.
The economic statement dealt with a number of things that will create hardship for the fishermen in my area. What about
Fisheries Act
the announcement of the possible cut-backs in unemployment insurance, for example? This is not the time to announce further restrictions on unemployment insurance. We have had a failure in the inshore fishery this year and after some prodding, the Government finally came forward with an amount of $6 million to help those people who did not receive the benefits that they required to carry on through the winter. That amount is inadequate. There are fishermen in small communities in Newfoundland who are still not able to draw unemployment insurance this year because the amount of $6 million which was made available after some prodding is inadequate. Now is no time to announce further restrictions on unemployment insurance.
As well, the Government cancelled certain capital projects like the marine service centre that was to be built at Smokey on the Labrador coast. The Government has announced that it will privatize insurance for long liners. That, I believe, is a disastrous move because if there were private industry companies that would insure those kinds of fishing vessels, they would have been doing so all along. I know of no alternative to government support for vessel insurance. I do not think there is any alternative. When the Minister was in Newfoundland, representatives from the fishermen's union spoke to him at length about this matter and told him that it presented them with a serious problem. I encourage the Minister to take a second look at his decision to privatize fishing vessel insurance because I believe it will have a disastrous effect on small inshore fishermen.
This is no time to make cut-backs in the fisheries policy because the industry is struggling. There is a great deal of competition in the market-place and particularly in the U.S. market-place. Scandivanian countries are putting a good quality product on the United States market at a reasonable cost thus creating a great deal of competition. This is no time to exercise those cut-backs on a struggling industry. Now is the time not for cut-backs but for incentives.
I want to know what the regional policy of the Government is. How is the Government going to ensure that small fishing firms, for example, in Atlantic Canada will have a fair chance in the market-place in the future? We have not heard from the Government on that issue. What is going to be done to help Fishery Products International? That company was set up when the private sector failed and it is owned now by both the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland. I believe it is going to need a further infusion of funds if it is to be financially sound and if it is going to be able to compete in the market-place. The Government has to tell us clearly what its policy is going to be with regard to Fishery Products International and how it intends to make it a sound financial operation.
In speaking of Fishery Products International, Mr. Speaker, I want to get on to a topic which is very important to me. That is the topic I raised with the Minister yesterday, the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation. This also was a recom-

March 6, 1985
Fisheries Act
mendation which came out of the Kirby report and it was accepted by both the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland. There was a signed agreement in principle to set up this Northern Fisheries Development Corporation north of 50 because it is understood that there are disadvantaged fishermen in that area who need special measures. It is not good enough to leave those plants on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland, such as St. Anthony, for example, and plants along the Labrador coast, at the mercy of Fisheries Products International. I believe that after the provincial election is over-whenever the Premier decides to call it and I feel it will come very soon-certain hard decisions will have to be taken with regard to Fishery Products International which are not going to be very easy to sell in my province.
I fear certain fish plant closures. I want to make sure that the people I represent, and the people on the northern peninsula and the Labrador coast, are taken care of. I would ask the Minister not to leave those people who live and fish in the north at the mercy of the people in the south. Those plants have been marginal. In the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador we have some of the most disadvantaged fishermen anywhere in Canada. The irony is that they have some of the greatest resources off their shores. There is cod, salmon, arctic char and shrimp resources off that coast. Yet those fishermen historically have been among the most disadvantaged in Canada.
A lot has been done to improve their lot and I don't want to get into that now, but more needs to be done, particularly in terms of marketing. We must help them to market their product. The whole reason behind the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation was basically to help them mobilize their catch and to receive a better deal in the market-place.
The Minister told me yesterday that there is no guarantee that the corporation will be in place by this fishing season. He told me that the money has been reallocated somewhere else. He did tell me that he was sympathetic and that is encouraging, but I want him to be more than sympathetic. I want the Minister to give people on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and on the coast of Labrador an assurance that he will follow through on that sympathy and that he will see that that Northern Fisheries Development Corporation is put in place, not some time in the future but this spring, before the next fishing season, because it is of paramount importance to those people. I hope the Minister will find time to consult with these people before he makes a final decision on this.
That, I think, sums up what I want to say on this Bill. It is a housekeeping Bill. It simply enshrines in law what the Department felt it could do all along. What I really want to see and what I am looking forward to is a chance to debate fisheries policy in this Chamber and in committee. Moreover, I would like a chance to see the fiscal framework of the Government so that we can put that policy into context. I would urge the Minister to bring forward that policy at the earliest possible opportunity and, of course, I would urge the Government to bring forward its fiscal statement so that we can see exactly
how the dollars and cents are going to affect those of us who live and work in Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member if any of these problems are new, and I believe none of them is. Since none of them is new, would the Hon. Member please explain to this House why they were not addressed when he was a member of the Cabinet; when the Crown Corporation was formed to look after the fishery; when the 200-mile limit was there and the northern resource was there? Are any of these problems new? If any of them are, would he delineate those and explain why the old ones were not addressed?
The remarks just made by the Hon. Member could very well have been taken from the debate on the Bill which created the Crown corporation. They could be taken from the remarks of Hon. Members on this side of the House when they were in opposition at the time the Bill was passed through the House and through committee. I appreciate the tone in which the Hon. Member has presented his remarks, but what is new?

Mr. Speaker, these are excellent questions. What is new, of course, is that there has been a suggestion that unemployment insurance will be restricted. That is new. There have been cut-backs in small craft harbours allocations, particularly in the $2 million infrastructure which was to be installed at Smokey. That is new. We had agreed to it; the present Government cancelled it. The fishing vessel insurance is going to be privatized. That is new. The Government was supporting it before. There was a government scheme to insure fishing vessels, which was the old policy. The new policy is that the Government will not do that but will hand it over to private enterprise. These are all new measures.
To speak particularly to the issue of the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation, the history of it is as follows. St. Anthony in particular was always a marginal plant under Fishery Products, fueled and supplied by the inshore fishery. It always lost money. As a matter of fact, it lost so much money that Fishery Products was going to close the plant down. The Government of Canada said; "We don't want that plant to close. It is the only receiver of fish products in that area of the northern peninsula so it must not close". So the Government of Canada under the then Minister of Fisheries, Mr. LeBlanc, who comes from the same province as the Hon. Member, said that he would ask the Canadian Saltfish Corporation if it would intervene. We had a great deal of trouble because the Province of Newfoundland got very upset that there was a federal intrusion into a provincial jurisdiction. It even threatened not to issue the fish processing licence for that plant.
However, that was overcome and the Canadian Saltfish Corporation took over that plant for a year. It ran the plant well and for the first time in history it broke even. The recommendation coming out of the Kirby report was that a Northern Fisheries Development Corporation be set up. We had the previous experience of the Canadian Saltfish Corporation. We had the vehicle in place and our idea-certainly my idea-was to allow the Canadian Saltfish Corporation to
March 6, 1985

operate that plant. But again, although the Government of Newfoundland signed an agreement in principle to set up a Northern Fisheries Development Corporation, it would not agree to have the Canadian Saltfish Corporation run it as such, or a subsidiary thereof. So negotiations have been going on with the Province of Newfoundland for all of that time to see if both Governments could come to an agreement as to how that corporation would be set up. I have seen nothing on paper in terms of a proposal from the Government of Newfoundland.
To answer the question directly, that is why action has not been taken. We were prepared to move. Indeed, we allocated $15 million for that particular project which, I gather now, has been reallocated to some other area or some other project. It is no longer there, although the Minister says, to give him his due, that he is sympathetic, and certainly if arrangements are concluded he will seek funds. I take him at his word. I hope that is a fair answer, Mr. Speaker, to what I believe is a very good question.

Mr. Speaker, two things are not new; he has made that very clear. Number one, with respect to public insurance versus private insurance, fishermen's organizations and clubs found that they could get better coverage from private sector insurance. Yes, they did.
Well, you ask Richard Cashin.
I am not interested in what Richard Cashin said. You know as well as I do the attitude he has taken on various occasions. He did not support either you or this side of the House.
But he does represent the fishermen.

There is a club in my constituency, so I know what I am talking about, which went the private route as a group for private insurance. They got their boats insured for replacement cost, which the public Act never would grant at any time. They accepted the value of the vessel as submitted by the manufacturer and the fisherman and insured the boat for that amount at less than the cost of public insurance. As long as there is that capability in the private sector, I submit it is not very logical for the public sector to continue the insurance unless it is prepared to match rates and coverage.
Two different experiences. It is not the same thing.
All right, but you mentioned Cashin and he goes the club route.
Let's not say Cashin; let's say the Newfoundland Fish, Food and Allied Workers' Union.

I submit that if they go the club route, or the union route which Mr. Cashin is associated with, then private insurance may very well give you, as it did in my constituency, better coverage for less money.
Fisheries Act
That is not the track record.

That is the existing track record, my friend. You speak of what you know and let me do the same thing without argument.
The second thing is there may have been a change in the amount of money for small craft harbours, but I want to tell you it has been awfully scarce in certain constituencies under the former Government and very plentiful in others. I hope this might be changed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Would the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) like another comment?

Mr. Speaker, no self-respecting politician would ever turn down the floor when it is offered by such a gracious person as yourself.
The two experiences, Mr. Speaker, are completely different. 1 appreciate that the Hon. Member speaks whereof he knows. I speak whereof I know, and that is what politics and representative government are all about. But the track record in Newfoundland is that there has not been that kind of support from the private sector for fishing vessel insurance at reasonable prices. The Government has provided the insurance and it is the position taken by the Fishermen's Union in Newfoundland, a very strong, powerful and large union, that this should not be changed. The Government should not depart from public support for fishing vessel insurance. To give it over to the private sector would be disastrous for people in a struggling industry at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The period of questions and comments is now terminated.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to place a few remarks on the record regarding Bill C-32. Before doing so I would like to say that I think that Members on both sides are very pleased with the appointment of the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser). There are great expectations all across the country because he has demonstrated in his years in this Chamber that when he takes on a task, he does it in a very sincere, honest and forthright way. I can certainly say that I have great respect for him and at the same time I have great expectations.
The matter of expectations is something I think the House has to look at in terms of Bill C-32. We have been requesting the appearance of the Minister before the committee, not only regarding Bill C-32 but also concerning the west coast salmon treaty, something which has very severe implications for some parts of my constituency and requires a great deal more evaluation than it has been given by our committee. Another matter has to do with insurance but we have not had the Minister in front of the committee on either of these issues. I know the Parliamentary Secretary is here and I am sure he would agree it would be inappropriate and inopportune to cancel the commercial fishing insurance program, and I think

Fisheries Act
that is how it will stay. But again we would like to hear from the Minister.
The Government side raised the problem of small craft harbours. We would like to know why vessels under 45 feet on the East Coast do not pay any berthage fees, yet all the fishermen I represent have been told their rates are going to be doubled. If I heard the Parliamentary Secretary correctly, he has just said that the rates in British Columbia are going to be brought into line with those on the East Coast very soon and I am pleased to hear that.
There are a couple of Trojan horse clauses in Bill C-32 which I think the House has to look at much more carefully than perhaps even the Minister has looked at them so far. Looking at the purposes clause, the first part, 2.1(a), provides for the conservation and protection of fish and waters frequented by fish. I think that is reasonable and expected. Part (b) is to provide for the proper management, allocation and control of the seacoast fisheries of Canada.
There we start to see the first wording of the Trojan horse clause. We find a distinction within the purposes clause of the Bill between the seacoast fishery and the inland fisheries. I intend to spend a few moments dealing with that.
Then, of course, Part (c), which is the contentious part and a point the Minister spent some time on relating to the Collier decisions. It refers to ensuring a continuing supply of fish and to maintaining and developing the economic and social benefits from the use of fish for fishermen and others employed in the Canadian seacoast fishing industry and for others whose livelihood depends in whole or in part on seacoast fishing, and for the people of Canada. That relates directly to the two Collier decisions.
I think the Minister outlined quite well the two decisions and I would just like to put a few remarks on the record regarding them. The first case involved the Fishing Vessel Owners' Association of B.C., the Pacific Coast Salmon Seiners Association and the Prince Rupert Fishing Vessel Owners' Association, and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. In that case Mr. Justice Collier granted an injunction preventing the Department from setting separate salmon quotas for seiners and gillnetters, prohibiting the Government from allocating the resource between gear types.
Strict interpretation of the Fisheries Act would then seem to say that all groups would have equal access to stocks over an equal area. The act gives the Department the power to enforce regulations for the preservation and conservation of the resource, but not to give preference to one user group over another on either social or economic grounds. Whatever the proper wording would be to give all due deference to Justice Collier and the Federal Court, I would side with the Minister in that I do not think a constitutional challenge would be successful once the amendment was in place with that wording.
The second case involved the Gulf Trollers Association of British Columbia versus the Department. In August of last year Mr. Justice Collier upheld the Association's application
to quash seven Government orders dated April 16 which permitted commercial fishing between July 1 and August 31, and at the same time allowing the sport fishers to operate year around. In effect this was allocating the resource by giving preference to one user group over another.
The Federal Court judge did not accept the Government's argument that it had federal power to manage and control the fisheries for the benefit of Canadians as distinct from preservation considerations. The April 16 variations of the total closure were, on the evidence presented by the Crown, conceived on two bases: a need for conservation, and the intention to favour the sport fishers. The conservation motive was at the ultimate expense of the commercial Gulf Trollers. The preference, the judge stated, was based on socio-economic considerations which he determined to be beyond the Department's permissible constitutional powers.
I would not want to put words into Justice Collier's mouth, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me that what he was trying to say was that it was beyond statutory or legislative powers as opposed to constitutional. The Minister touched on the very delicate dilemma this country would find itself in if it was impossible for different Ministries, either at the federal or provincial levels or in fact at the municipal or aboriginal self-government levels, to manage the resource for social or economic reasons. I think we would have a rather chaotic Constitution which would be the same length as the Income Tax Act, some 34 feet in length, if we had constitutional debates about the ability of Parliament to pass statutes to allow the division of such things as the fishery.
I would like to deal with what I consider to be the Trojan horse clauses of this Bill which make it so important for the Minister to come before the committee to explain. In Clause 1 he added "portions of fish". That is quite understandable. He has also added "marine plants and portions thereof'. I think that is good. There has been a debate in British Columbia as to whether the Government of B.C. can issue kelp harvesting permits and that type of thing. I think this will certainly clarify that.
Clause 2.1(d) says:
to provide, in cooperation with the provinces, for the proper management, allocation and control of the inland fisheries of Canada.
It is quite clear from some available judgments that once you get out of tidal waters you are getting into inland waters. The Minister must tell the committee and those interested in this particular matter exactly what his intention is in bringing the provinces in in terms of "the proper management, allocation and control". I am sure many Members of the House are aware that under the west coast salmon treaty on the Fraser river there is a very specific, internationally recognized allocation of 400,000 pieces for the native food fishery on the Fraser River system. That same allocation is not found on any river system in B.C. other that the Fraser. In British Columbia we will find ourselves with a government which will not recognize

aboriginal rights or title. In fact, it will not even appoint a Minister responsible for that matter.
How can discussions regarding inland fisheries possibly proceed with that kind of wording inserted? The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has a responsibility to come before the committee and explain fully why he has added that particular wording and what the implications are for negotiations regarding the native food fishery in Canada and possibly, in the future, inland commercialized fisheries of native people, which is an aboriginal right recognized in the Constitution.
I would like to discuss some of the other difficulties we are faced with, not having had the Minister before the committee. The basic problem with the Bill is that we cannot discuss these things with the Minister but must discuss them in Parliament before the public of Canada. The buy-back is crucial. The Minister is on record, as are many other Conservatives who were elected to this place, as saying that there will be a $100 million buy-back within the B.C. fishing industry this year. It is not included in the Estimates. I assume that the money will be found somewhere. Perhaps it will come from the Department of Transport or another department. We are eager to hear from the Minister where the money will come from.
The second matter is the $200 million salmon enhancement program. These amendments dovetail with the possible implications of the salmon enhancement program. This basically has to do with the division of stock on the B.C. coast and in the Maritimes of Canada, whether it be lobster, salmon, crab, oolichans, geoducks or kelp which is included in this amendment. We must have some understanding of the direction the Department is taking with these major agenda items which will have an effect on the global stock productions.
I would like to spend a moment on one of the key problems. We do not know how soon the money for the buy-back or the salmon enhancement program will come. We do not know what the implications of these clauses will be in terms of consitutional negotiations with our aboriginal people. We do not have a clear understanding of why the Minister smuggled in an amendment to paragraph 34(m) which says:
authorizing a person engaged or employed in the administration or enforcement of this Act to vary, in respect of any area or portion thereof, any close time, fishing quota or limit on the size or weight of fish that has been fixed by the regulations.
This power is beyond anything anyone in the House has yet imagined. This is government by regulation. Someone who is hired for 30 days by DFO working out of Come-By-Chance, Prince Rupert, or Tofino could well make a sudden decision that you cannot keep Chinook under 50 pounds, or that a particular creek is going to be closed, or that lobsters cannot be taken for some particular reason. These kinds of authorizations should be far more specific and explicit rather than merely putting in a clause which allows a person working for DFO to do anything. It directly affects the income of everyone involved in the industry.
This is really the crux of the matter. We do not know about the insurance, salmon enhancement, the buy-back, the consti-
Fisheries Act
tutional implications of the west coast treaty or of this amendment.
However, the other very serious and chronic problem of the Department with regard to the industry itself must be addressed by the House. We do not have a good enough understanding of what the maximum potential spawning yield or the maximum habitat potential of the streams is. We do not understand what the maximum return of the various wild stocks is or what the implication of adding hatchery stocks to those stocks is going to be. We do not know about these things in terms of kelp, oolichans or a lot of other species. There has not been enough time, energy or research effort put into determining what the global stocks can be. We know that they are now devastated on the East and West Coasts. We need to know how we can develop the resource and what our maximum yield and utilization can be so that we can discover what the social and economic impacts are for the different gear types. If negotiations are going to take place this year with aboriginal groups in the country, we need to know what a realistic negotiated settlement can be that can then be constitutionally protected.
In order to do that we need proper tagging programs and proper stream and creek evaluation. We need a firm understanding of the implications of major projects such as the CN twin-tracking. We will then not have to deal with the no net loss policies and the net gain because we will know where the dollars are going to be spent and what the returns are going to be much more accurately than we do now. We will not have to worry about the voodoo-like predictions of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
Fishermen often wonder whether specific areas will be open, whether they will be able to take pinks, whether the Gulf will be closed, and how many herring they will be allowed to take and what size they must be. It is treated very much like voodoo, Mr. Speaker. The fishermen on the coast do not know from day to day whether there will be a buy-back. They do not know whether there will be an opening or closing. They do not know if their insurance will be taken away.
The Department has been placed in that state of chaos by a run of Ministers who, I firmly believe, did not put the kind of energy into the Department that was required. I think that the present Minister has that potential, but he needs the support of his front-bench colleagues to get the cash. I am sure that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) will be fighting in Cabinet to ensure that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans gets that funding.
What about the Minister of Transport?

The Minister of Transport needs the cash too, he says. However, Fisheries and Oceans is crucial.
I will conclude my remarks by pointing out that before Parliament should consider passing this Bill, it and the Minister should appear before the committee. The Minister should explain its contents and the constitutional and statutory implications of it as related to the Collier decision. He should
